verse.text: The book of the origin of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.

note.traditional: The book of the genealogy (or “generation”) of Jesus Christ

verse.note: The Greek word is the one that gives the first book of the Bible its name, and the phrase echoes the Greek of Genesis 2:4 and 5:1. Most translations render it “genealogy” here and “birth” in verse 18. “Origin” is used in both places so that the reader can see Matthew using the same word twice. Whether the heading covers the genealogy only, the opening chapters or the whole book is disputed.

verse.text: Abraham fathered Isaac, Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers.
Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, Perez fathered Hezron, and Hezron fathered Ram.
verse.note: Jewish genealogies normally ran through fathers only. Matthew names four mothers before Mary—Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and “Uriah’s wife” (Bathsheba)—passing over the famous matriarchs. Why he chose these four is debated; common suggestions are that they were foreigners or linked to foreigners, or that each became a mother in the royal line in irregular circumstances, preparing the reader for Mary.

verse.text: Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, and Nahshon fathered Salmon.
Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, and Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David the king. David fathered Solomon by Uriah’s wife.
Solomon fathered Rehoboam, Rehoboam fathered Abijah, and Abijah fathered Asaph.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “Asaph” here and “Amos” in verse 10, where the Old Testament kings are Asa and Amon; later manuscripts have the expected names. Many English versions print “Asa” and “Amon”. This translation follows the Greek text as edited. Whether Matthew used variant spellings of the kings’ names or intended an allusion to the psalmist and the prophet is uncertain.

verse.text: Asaph fathered Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat fathered Joram, and Joram fathered Uzziah.
Uzziah fathered Jotham, Jotham fathered Ahaz, and Ahaz fathered Hezekiah.
Hezekiah fathered Manasseh, Manasseh fathered Amos, and Amos fathered Josiah.
Josiah fathered Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon.
After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel, and Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel.
Zerubbabel fathered Abiud, Abiud fathered Eliakim, and Eliakim fathered Azor.
Azor fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Achim, and Achim fathered Eliud.
Eliud fathered Eleazar, Eleazar fathered Matthan, and Matthan fathered Jacob.
Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called the Messiah.
verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew “Messiah”, the anointed king Israel expected. Where it functions as a title, as here and in verse 17, this translation uses “Messiah”; where it is attached to “Jesus” as part of his name (verses 1 and 18), it uses “Christ”. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

After thirty-nine repetitions of “fathered”, the pattern breaks: Joseph is not said to have fathered Jesus. The verb turns passive, and “of whom” is feminine singular in Greek, referring to Mary alone. The rest of the chapter explains the break.

verse.text: So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Messiah fourteen generations.
verse.note: The list is shaped to give three groups of fourteen; for example, three kings known from the Old Testament are passed over between Joram and Uzziah, and the third group has fourteen names only if Jeconiah is counted again. A widely held suggestion is that fourteen is the sum of the Hebrew letters of the name David, but Matthew does not say so and the explanation is not certain.

verse.text: Now the origin of Jesus Christ was like this. His mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, but before they came together she was found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: Jewish betrothal was a binding legal contract, much more than a modern engagement. The couple were already called husband and wife (verses 19–20), unfaithfulness counted as adultery, and the bond could be ended only by divorce. The marriage was completed, often about a year later, when the husband took the bride into his home, which is what “take home” refers to in verses 20 and 24.

verse.text: Joseph her husband, being a righteous man and not wanting to expose her to public disgrace, decided to divorce her quietly.
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice); here the word describes a man who keeps God’s law. The connection with what follows can be read two ways: because he was righteous he could not go through with the marriage but chose the kindest way out, or although he was righteous he did not want to shame her. The translation leaves both open.

verse.text: But when he had thought this over, look, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and said, “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take home Mary your wife, for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

text.q: She will give birth to a son, and you are to name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”

verse.note: “Jesus” is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yeshua, a shortened form of Joshua, which was understood to mean “the Lord saves”. The angel’s explanation, “for he will save his people”, plays on that meaning. The wordplay works in Hebrew or Aramaic and is not visible in Greek or English.

verse.text: All this took place to fulfill what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet:
“Look, the virgin will become pregnant and give birth to a son, and they will name him Emmanuel,” which is translated “God with us.”
verse.note: Matthew quotes Isaiah 7:14 in its Greek form, where the word normally means a virgin. The Hebrew of Isaiah has a word meaning a young woman of marriageable age, which does not in itself specify virginity. Isaiah has “you will call” or “she will call” where Matthew has “they will name”.

verse.text: When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and took his wife home,
but he did not have sexual relations with her until she had given birth to a son, and he named him Jesus.

note.term: did not have sexual relations with her until

verse.note: The Greek says literally that he “did not know her”, a biblical idiom for sexual intercourse. “Until” fixes what was true up to the birth and does not by itself say what happened afterward. Most Protestant interpreters take it to imply normal marital relations later, while Catholic and Orthodox tradition holds that Mary remained a virgin; the Greek does not settle it. Some later manuscripts read “her firstborn son”, probably taken from Luke 2:7.

verse.text: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod, magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem,
verse.note: The Greek word named a class of eastern (originally Persian) priest-scholars known for astrology and dream interpretation; it could also mean “magician,” as in Acts 13. “Wise men” is vaguer than the Greek and hides the link to star-watching that drives the story. Several modern versions also use “Magi.” The text does not say how many there were or call them kings.

This is Herod the Great, who ruled Judea as a client king under Rome and is generally thought to have died in 4 BC. He was known for his suspicion of rivals, which included executing members of his own family.

verse.text: asking, “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star at its rising and have come to pay him homage.”
verse.note: In verse 1 the plural of this word without the article means “the east.” Here and in verse 9 it is singular with the article, which most scholars now take as the astronomical term for a star’s rising above the horizon. “In the east” remains possible and is kept by some versions.

The verb means to prostrate oneself in reverence, and what it implies depends on the recipient. Here foreign visitors honor a newborn king, and verse 11 states the falling down separately, so “pay homage” is used in verses 2, 8 and 11. Translations are divided: NRSV has “pay homage,” while KJV, NIV and ESV have “worship,” and many readers see Matthew hinting at more than royal honor.

verse.text: When King Herod heard this he was alarmed, and all Jerusalem with him,
and gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Messiah was to be born.
verse.note: Herod is asking about a title, the anointed king Israel expected, not using a name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader where “Christ” can sound like a surname. Several modern translations make the same choice in passages like this one.

verse.text: They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is what is written through the prophet:

text.q: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.’”

verse.note: The quotation is from Micah 5:2, with the final line about shepherding God’s people echoing 2 Samuel 5:2, words spoken to David. Matthew’s wording differs from both the Hebrew and the Greek Old Testament, which call Bethlehem small among the clans of Judah; here its littleness is denied because of the ruler who comes from it.

verse.text: Then Herod secretly summoned the magi and carefully ascertained from them the time when the star had appeared,
and sending them to Bethlehem he said, “Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and pay him homage.”
After hearing the king they set out, and there ahead of them went the star they had seen at its rising, until it came and stood over the place where the child was.
When they saw the star, they rejoiced with very great joy.
Entering the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and paid him homage. Then they opened their treasure chests and offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
And having been warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they withdrew to their own country by another road.

After they had withdrawn, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, “Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and stay there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child to destroy him.”
So he got up, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt,
and he was there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

note.term: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

verse.note: The words are from Hosea 11:1, where “my son” is Israel brought out of Egypt in the exodus. Matthew presents Jesus as retracing Israel’s story. “Son” is left lowercase so that the quotation keeps both its original reference and Matthew’s application.

verse.text: Then Herod, seeing that he had been made a fool of by the magi, was furious, and he sent and put to death all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its surrounding district who were two years old and under, in keeping with the time he had carefully ascertained from the magi.
verse.note: The Greek noun is masculine plural, which can mean “boys” specifically or “children” of both sexes. Since Herod is hunting a male rival, most modern translations and commentators understand “boys.” The KJV has “children.”

verse.text: Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:

text.q: “A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great lamentation—Rachel weeping for her children, and she refused to be comforted, because they are no more.”

verse.note: The quotation is Jeremiah 31:15. Rachel, wife of Jacob and a mother of Israel, was by tradition buried near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19), and Ramah was a town north of Jerusalem associated with the deportation of exiles to Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1). Jeremiah pictures her mourning the exiles, and Matthew applies the image to the mothers of Bethlehem.

verse.text: When Herod had died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt
and said, “Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child’s life have died.”

note.term: those who were seeking the child’s life have died

verse.note: The wording, including the plural “those” when only Herod has died, closely echoes Exodus 4:19, where God tells Moses to return to Egypt because those who sought his life are dead. The echo is one of several parallels this chapter draws between Jesus and Moses.

verse.text: So he got up, took the child and his mother, and entered the land of Israel.
But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. Having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the region of Galilee,
verse.note: At Herod’s death his kingdom was divided among his sons. Archelaus received Judea with the lesser title of ethnarch and was removed by Rome in AD 6 after complaints about his rule. Galilee went to his brother Herod Antipas.

verse.text: and he came and settled in a town called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.

note.term: that he would be called a Nazarene
note.traditional: He shall be called a Nazarene

verse.note: No Old Testament passage contains these words, and Matthew speaks of “the prophets” in the plural without his usual “saying,” so the clause is rendered here as a summary, not a direct quotation. What he has in mind is disputed: common proposals are a wordplay on the Hebrew for “branch” in Isaiah 11:1, an allusion to the Nazirite of Judges 13:5, or the general prophetic theme of a despised servant. The Greek form is strictly “Nazorean,” which Matthew plainly connects with Nazareth.

verse.text: In those days John the Baptist came, proclaiming in the wilderness of Judea
and saying, “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repent,” which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word, as used in the Gospels, carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. The related noun in verses 8 and 11 is rendered “turning back.”

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that most translations flatten to “heaven.” The expression is characteristic of Matthew and is generally understood as equivalent to “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels, with “the heavens” standing reverently for God.

The Greek perfect tense says that the kingdom has drawn near and now stands close. Whether this means it is about to arrive or has in some sense already arrived is debated; the rendering leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: For this is the one spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, who said: “A voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’”

note.term: A voice of one crying out in the wilderness

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 40:3 in the form found in the Greek translation of the Scriptures (the Septuagint). In the Hebrew text “in the wilderness” more naturally goes with “prepare the way”; the Greek form, attaching it to the voice, fits John’s location. “His paths” replaces Isaiah’s “the paths of our God.”

verse.text: Now John himself wore clothing made of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.

note.term: a leather belt around his waist

verse.note: John’s dress recalls the description of the prophet Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8, a hairy garment and a leather belt. A reader who knew the Scriptures would have caught the allusion, which Matthew later makes explicit when Jesus identifies John with Elijah.

verse.text: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan were going out to him,
and they were being baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.
But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?
verse.note: The Greek can mean that they came in order to be baptized or simply that they came to the place where John was baptizing, perhaps to observe. John’s sharp response fits either reading, and the rendering keeps the Greek’s openness.

text.q: So produce fruit worthy of turning back,
and do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones.
Already the ax is laid at the root of the trees; so every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
I baptize you in water for turning back, but the one coming after me is stronger than I am, and I am not fit to carry his sandals. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mark either the element in which someone is immersed (“in”) or the means used (“with”), and translations are divided. “In” is chosen because the verb’s ordinary sense is to dip or immerse; the same preposition is rendered the same way for “in the Holy Spirit and fire.”
Carrying or removing a master’s sandals was a task for a slave. John is saying he is not worthy to perform even the lowliest service for the one who is coming.

text.q: His winnowing shovel is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”

verse.note: Most modern translations have “winnowing fork,” but the Greek word names the shovel used to toss threshed grain into the wind so that the light chaff blows away and the heavier grain falls to the floor; a different word was used for the fork. The image is the same either way: the harvest is in and the separation is about to begin.

verse.text: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.
But John tried to stop him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”
But Jesus answered him, “Allow it for now, for in this way it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him.
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). In Matthew the word usually refers to doing what God requires, and here most interpreters take “fulfill all righteousness” to mean carrying out everything God’s will calls for. Some see instead a reference to God’s saving plan being brought to completion.

verse.text: When Jesus had been baptized, he came up at once from the water; and look, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.

note.traditional: the heavens were opened to him

verse.note: Many manuscripts add “to him” after “opened,” while some important early witnesses lack it. The text translated here follows the shorter reading; the difference affects whether the opening is presented as something Jesus in particular perceived.

verse.text: And look, a voice from the heavens, saying, “This is my Son, the beloved, with whom I am well pleased.”
verse.note: The words echo Psalm 2:7 (“You are my son”) and Isaiah 42:1 (the servant in whom God delights). In the Greek Scriptures “beloved” used of a son can carry the nuance of an only child, as with Isaac in Genesis 22:2.

verse.text: Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit, to be tested by the devil.
verse.note: Most translations have “tempted” here. The Greek verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for God testing Israel in the wilderness, the background this scene draws on. Modern “tempt” has narrowed to enticing someone to sin, which hides that link; lexicons recognize both senses, and which fits best here is disputed. The same verb lies behind “the tempter” in verse 3, and a compound of it behind “put to the test” in verse 7.

verse.text: After fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry.
And the tempter came up and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become loaves of bread.”
But he answered, “It is written: ‘A person shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes out through the mouth of God.’”
verse.note: All three of Jesus’ replies come from Deuteronomy 6–8 (8:3; 6:16; 6:13), where Moses looks back on Israel’s forty years of testing in the wilderness. A reader who knew the Scriptures would have heard Jesus’ forty days as a reliving of that story. The devil’s own quotation in verse 6 is from Psalm 91:11–12.

verse.text: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple,
verse.note: The Greek word was used for a projecting edge or tip, and here names some high point of the temple complex; exactly which part is unknown. The traditional “pinnacle” is kept, though a spire should not be imagined. Suggestions include a corner of the outer wall above the Kidron valley or the edge of the sanctuary roof.

verse.text: and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written: ‘He will command his angels concerning you, and on their hands they will lift you up, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone.’”
Jesus said to him, “Again it is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”
Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,
and he said to him, “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.”
Then Jesus said to him, “Go away, Satan! For it is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”
Then the devil left him, and look, angels came and waited on him.
verse.note: The verb’s everyday sense is to attend to someone’s needs, especially by serving food, which fits the end of a forty-day fast. “Ministered” now sounds religious and vague. “Served” was avoided only because it has just been used in verse 10 for a different Greek verb meaning religious service to God.

verse.text: When he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee.
verse.note: Most translations say John was “arrested” or “put in prison.” The Greek verb simply means to hand someone over into another’s power, and Matthew uses the same word later for what happens to Jesus and what will happen to his disciples. Rendering it the same way throughout lets the reader see that chain. The imprisonment itself is described in Matthew 14:3.

verse.text: And leaving Nazareth, he went and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,
so that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled:

text.q: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles—

verse.note: One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples; this translation renders it “Gentiles” or “nations” according to sense, and “Galilee of the nations” is also possible here. The quotation is from Isaiah 9:1–2, which speaks of northern territories that fell early to Assyrian conquest.

text.q: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light, and on those sitting in the region and shadow of death a light has dawned.”

verse.text: From then on Jesus began to proclaim and say, “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”
verse.note: “Repent” is the traditional rendering, and most translations keep it as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English, though, the word centers on feeling sorry. The Greek carries the prophets’ call to “return” to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, which “turn back” conveys.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew, and a first-century hearer would have noticed it. Most translations flatten it to “the kingdom of heaven.” The phrase is generally taken as equivalent to “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels.

verse.text: As he was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
And he said to them, “Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of people.”
verse.note: The Greek word means human beings in general, not males, so “people” is more accurate than the traditional “men.” The phrase plays on “fishermen” in the previous verse, which is the same Greek noun.

verse.text: At once they left their nets and followed him.
Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them.
At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.
He went around all of Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every ailment among the people.
verse.note: “Gospel” has become a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, also used of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

verse.text: News of him spread throughout all Syria, and they brought to him all who were ill, those suffering from various diseases and severe pains, those possessed by demons, those who had seizures, and the paralyzed, and he healed them.
verse.note: The Greek word is built on the word for “moon” and reflects the ancient belief that the moon caused the condition. In Matthew 17:15 the same word describes a boy who falls into fire and water, so recurring seizures are in view. Many modern versions have “epileptics”; “seizures” describes the symptoms without importing a modern diagnosis.

verse.text: And large crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.
When he saw the crowds, he went up the mountain, and after he sat down, his disciples came to him.
Then he opened his mouth and began to teach them, saying:

text.q: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of the heavens.

verse.note: Matthew's Greek has the plural, “the heavens,” reflecting the Hebrew and Aramaic word for heaven, which is always plural. Most English versions flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept here, and in “your Father in the heavens,” because a first-century hearer would have recognized it as a Semitic turn of phrase.

text.q: Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.
Blessed are the gentle, for they will inherit the earth.

verse.note: “Meek” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone gentle, humble and not self-assertive, and “gentle” or “humble” is the usual modern rendering. The verse echoes Psalm 37:11, where the same Greek word in the Septuagint stands for the humble poor who will inherit “the land”; the Greek word translated “earth” here can mean either.

text.q: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied.

verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The word covers both being in the right before God and doing what is right. Translations into most other languages use their word for “justice” throughout, and some scholars prefer “justice” in English as well.

text.q: Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.
Blessed are those who have been persecuted for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of the heavens.
Blessed are you when people insult you and persecute you and falsely say every kind of evil against you because of me.
Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in the heavens; for that is how they persecuted the prophets who came before you.
You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its taste, with what will it be salted? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people.

verse.note: The Greek verb ordinarily means “become foolish” or “make foolish.” Here and in Luke 14:34 it is used of salt that has become insipid and useless. A Greek hearer may well have caught the double sense, a warning against disciples who become fools; some scholars suggest an underlying Aramaic wordplay, but that is uncertain.

text.q: You are the light of the world. A city set on top of a mountain cannot be hidden.
Nor do people light a lamp and put it under the measuring basket, but on the lampstand, and it shines for everyone in the house.
In the same way, let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in the heavens.
Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill.
For truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one stroke of a letter, will pass away from the Law until everything has taken place.

note.term: not one iota, not one stroke of a letter

verse.note: Iota is the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet and here stands for yod, the smallest Hebrew letter. The “stroke” (literally “little horn”) is a small mark or projection on a letter; exactly which feature of the script is meant is debated. The point is that not even the smallest detail of the Law will lapse.

text.q: So whoever sets aside one of the least of these commandments and teaches people to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of the heavens.
For I tell you that unless your righteousness goes far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of the heavens.
You have heard that it was said to the people of old, ‘You shall not murder, and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; and whoever says to his brother, ‘Raka,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool!’ will be liable to the Gehenna of fire.

note.traditional: angry with his brother without a cause

verse.note: Many manuscripts add “without cause” after “brother,” and the King James Version follows them. The words are absent from several of the earliest witnesses, and most editors judge them an early addition meant to soften the saying. The shorter text is translated here.

Matthew leaves this Aramaic insult untranslated in his Greek, so it is left as it stands here. It is a term of contempt, probably meaning something like “empty-head.” The “council” is a judicial body; the word is also used for the high council in Jerusalem, the Sanhedrin.

Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom beside Jerusalem, which the prophets associated with child sacrifice and coming judgment and which by the first century had become a name for the place of final punishment. Many translations render it “hell,” usually with a footnote giving the name. The name is kept here because “hell” merges it with Hades, a different word, and with later imagery.

text.q: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you,
leave your gift there in front of the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Come to terms quickly with your opponent at law while you are with him on the road, or your opponent may hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison.
Truly I tell you, you will never get out of there until you have paid back the last penny.
You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’
But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

verse.note: The Greek expresses purpose: looking with the aim of desiring. The verb is the one the Septuagint uses in the commandment “You shall not covet your neighbor's wife,” and the word for “woman” can also mean “wife,” so the saying may have another man's wife specifically in view. Most translations render “lustfully” or “with lust,” which can suggest that any passing attraction is meant.

text.q: If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; for it is better for you to lose one of your members than for your whole body to be thrown into Gehenna.

verse.note: The verb comes from the Septuagint's word for a trap or obstacle and means to trip someone up so that they fall away from loyalty to God. The King James “offend” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak. Modern versions divide between “cause to stumble” and “cause to sin”; the first is used here because it keeps the picture and is not limited to a single act of sin.

text.q: And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; for it is better for you to lose one of your members than for your whole body to go off into Gehenna.
It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife must give her a certificate of divorce.’
But I tell you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

note.term: except on the ground of sexual immorality
note.traditional: saving for the cause of fornication

verse.note: The Greek word is a broad term for unlawful sexual intercourse of any kind. Most interpreters take it here to mean sexual unfaithfulness by the wife. Others have argued for a narrower reference, such as marriages within the degrees of kinship forbidden in Leviticus 18 or unchastity before marriage; the question remains disputed.

text.q: Again, you have heard that it was said to the people of old, ‘You shall not break an oath, but shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’
But I tell you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is God’s throne;
nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.
And do not swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.
Let your word be ‘Yes, yes’ or ‘No, no’; anything more than these comes from the evil one.
You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’
But I tell you, do not resist the one who is evil. Instead, whoever slaps you on the right cheek, turn the other to him as well;

verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil person”) or neuter (“evil”). The examples that follow, a slap, a lawsuit, a forced march, point to a person who does wrong to you. Some scholars also argue that “resist” here means specifically to retaliate by force or in court. The same form in verse 37 is rendered “the evil one,” meaning the devil, though “evil” is possible there as well.

text.q: and if anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well;
and whoever presses you into service for one mile, go with him two.

verse.note: The verb is a technical term, Persian in origin, for the right of officials and soldiers to requisition civilians and their animals to carry loads. The same word is used when Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross in Matthew 27:32. Hearers in Roman-occupied Galilee would have known the practice at first hand.

text.q: Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.
You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’

verse.note: “Love your neighbor” is from Leviticus 19:18, but “hate your enemy” is not found in Scripture. It appears to summarize a common inference that the command to love applied only to one's own people. Comparable language about hating outsiders is found in the Dead Sea Scrolls.

text.q: But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

note.term: pray for those who persecute you
note.traditional: bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you

verse.note: Many later manuscripts have a longer form of this verse, adding blessing those who curse you and doing good to those who hate you. The additions appear to have been brought in from the parallel in Luke 6:27–28. The earliest manuscripts have the shorter text translated here.

text.q: so that you may become children of your Father in the heavens; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.
For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?
And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?
So you are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

verse.note: The Greek word means complete, whole or fully grown, and in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew for being wholehearted or blameless before God (for example Deuteronomy 18:13). In context it describes love that is undivided, extending to enemies as God's does, more than moral flawlessness in the abstract. “Perfect” is kept because the comparison is with God, but “complete” or “whole” are defensible renderings.

text.q: Be careful not to practice your righteousness in front of people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in the heavens.

verse.note: Here the word means the practice of religious duty; the three examples that follow are giving to the needy, prayer and fasting. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), and some scholars prefer “justice”. Some later manuscripts read “almsgiving” in this verse, which is why the King James Version has “alms”.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 9, a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. Where the Greek is singular (verses 10 and 20) the text has “heaven”, and it has “sky” where the visible sky is meant (verse 26).

text.q: So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be praised by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a stage actor, and in this passage the picture of a performance is active: a trumpet, street corners, an audience. Jewish Greek before the New Testament already used the word for a godless or insincere person, which is why most translations have “hypocrites” here. “Performers” is used in verses 2, 5 and 16 because the charge in each case is doing religion in order to be seen.

note.term: they have been paid their reward in full

verse.note: The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts of the period for payment received in full, so hearers would have caught a commercial tone: the account is settled and nothing more is owed. Older translations have “they have their reward”; many modern ones have “they have received their reward in full”.

text.q: But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,
so that your giving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

And when you pray, you must not be like the performers, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the main streets, so that they may be seen by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.
But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.
And when you pray, do not babble on like the Gentiles, for they think that they will be heard because of their many words.

note.traditional: use vain repetitions; heap up empty phrases

verse.note: The Greek verb is very rare and its exact sense is uncertain; it may imitate the sound of stammering or meaningless chatter. The next clause, about “many words”, shows that the fault is wordiness meant to win a hearing. Other translations have “use vain repetitions” or “heap up empty phrases”.

text.q: So do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
Pray, then, in this way: ‘Our Father in the heavens, may your name be held holy,

note.term: may your name be held holy

verse.note: The verb is built on the ordinary Greek word for “holy”. With God’s name as its object it means to treat or acknowledge as holy, not to make holy. “Hallowed” says the same thing but is no longer current English; the meaning is not in dispute. Many scholars take the passive as a request that God himself bring this about.

text.q: may your kingdom come, may your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.
Give us today our daily bread.

verse.note: The Greek word is almost unknown outside the Lord’s Prayer and its meaning is uncertain. The main proposals are “for the coming day”, “necessary for existence” and “for today”. With no secure alternative, the traditional “daily” is kept.

text.q: And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
And do not bring us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one.’

verse.note: In the usage of the period, including the Greek Old Testament, the word chiefly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will stay faithful. English “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin and could suggest that God lures people into wrongdoing. Most versions keep “temptation” and some have “time of trial”; scholars disagree about which sense is in view here, so this rendering is an editorial choice.

The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil one”, meaning the devil) or neuter (“evil”). The traditional wording of the prayer has “evil”. Many modern translations and scholars prefer “the evil one”, since Matthew uses the same expression for the devil elsewhere (13:19, 13:38), but the question remains open.

note.term: rescue us from the evil one

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add a closing doxology: “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.” It is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is generally regarded as a later addition from the prayer’s use in worship, so it is not part of the Greek text translated here.

text.q: For if you forgive people their offenses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you;

verse.note: The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. The traditional “trespasses” now chiefly suggests entering property without permission. It is a different word from “debts” in verse 12, which reflects a Jewish way of speaking of sins as debts owed to God.

text.q: but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your offenses.

And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the performers, for they make their faces unsightly so that they may be seen by people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.
But you, when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,
so that you may be seen to be fasting not by people but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.
Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal;

verse.note: The Greek word literally means “eating”. It may refer to the corrosion of metal, which is the traditional understanding, or to insects or vermin that eat stored goods, as some modern translations take it.

text.q: but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in or steal.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light;

verse.note: The Greek word means single or sincere, and related words are used of open-handed giving. The saying stands between treasure in heaven and slavery to wealth, and it is paired with the “evil eye”, a known idiom for stinginess, so “generous” fits the context. Most translations have “healthy” or “sound”, keeping the physical picture of an eye that lets in light, and mention generosity in a footnote; that picture is less visible in this rendering.

text.q: but if your eye is stingy, your whole body will be full of darkness. So if the light in you is darkness, how great that darkness is!

verse.note: The Greek says “evil”. An “evil eye” is a Jewish idiom for a grudging, tight-fisted attitude (for example Deuteronomy 15:9; compare Matthew 20:15). Most translations have “evil”, “bad” or “unhealthy”, which keeps the physical image; the rendering here follows from “generous” in verse 22.

text.q: No one can be a slave to two masters, for he will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot be slaves to God and to wealth.

verse.note: The verb means to serve as a slave, someone wholly owned by a master. Most translations have “serve”, which is accurate but lets a modern reader picture a job that could be split between two employers.

The Greek keeps an Aramaic word for wealth or property, traditionally carried into English as “Mammon”; modern translations have “money” or “wealth”. The saying pictures it as a rival master, but there is no evidence that it was the name of a deity.

text.q: For this reason I tell you: do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?
Look at the birds of the sky: they do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they are?
And which of you by worrying can add a single hour to your span of life?

note.term: a single hour to your span of life

verse.note: The Greek says “add one cubit”, a length of about eighteen inches, to a word that can mean either age or height. The King James Version has “one cubit unto his stature”. Most modern translations take the cubit as a figure for a short stretch of time added to a lifespan, since the saying calls for a small addition, not a large one.

text.q: And why do you worry about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor or spin.
Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.
But if this is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, you of little faith?
So do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’
For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all.

verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples, and it is translated “Gentiles” or “nations” according to context. In verse 7 “Gentiles” translates a closely related adjective.

text.q: But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “the kingdom of God and his righteousness”. The Greek text translated here has only “the kingdom and his righteousness”, where “his” refers to the Father of verse 32 and is taken to apply to both nouns.

text.q: So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.
“Do not judge, so that you will not be judged.
For you will be judged by the judgment with which you judge, and it will be measured to you by the measure with which you measure.

verse.note: The passive verbs do not name who does the judging and measuring. Most interpreters take them as a reverent way of referring to God’s judgment, a common idiom in Jewish speech of the period. They could also be read as a general observation that people are treated as they treat others.

text.q: Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?

verse.note: The Greek word names a main structural timber of a building, such as a roof beam, and the word for “speck” a tiny chip of straw or wood. The contrast is a deliberately absurd exaggeration.

text.q: Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ and look, the beam is in your own eye?
You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.
“Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls in front of pigs, or they will trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.

verse.note: The phrase most naturally suggests consecrated food, such as meat from a sacrifice, which only certain people could eat. Dogs were mostly scavengers, not pets, and pigs were unclean animals under the Law of Moses, so both stand for those with no regard for what is sacred. Who exactly is meant is not stated and is disputed.

text.q: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
Or is there anyone among you who, when his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?
Or when he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?
If you, then, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in the heavens give good things to those who ask him!

verse.note: The Greek is plural here and in verse 21, reflecting a Semitic way of speaking about God’s dwelling that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. The plural is kept wherever the Greek has it.

text.q: “So everything you want people to do for you, do the same for them; for this is the Law and the Prophets.
“Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and spacious the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it.
For narrow is the gate and cramped the road that leads to life, and few are those who find it.

verse.note: The edition translated here reads “for” (ὅτι), parallel to verse 13. Many manuscripts and some critical editions instead read a word (τί) that makes the sentence an exclamation: “How narrow is the gate!” The sense of the saying is little affected.

The participle means “pressed in” or “squeezed”, the opposite of the “spacious” road of verse 13. The same verb is used elsewhere of people under pressure or persecution. Many translations therefore render it “hard” or “difficult”, and a hearer may have caught both senses.

text.q: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.
You will recognize them by their fruits. Do people gather grapes from thornbushes, or figs from thistles?
In the same way, every good tree produces fine fruit, but the rotten tree produces bad fruit.
A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a rotten tree produce fine fruit.
Every tree that does not produce fine fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
So then, you will recognize them by their fruits.
“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of the heavens, but the one who does the will of my Father in the heavens.
Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, was it not in your name that we prophesied, and in your name that we drove out demons, and in your name that we did many deeds of power?’

verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for “power” used of concrete acts. There is no dispute about the meaning, and “miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering. “Deeds of power” is used throughout this translation so that the link with the word “power” stays visible.

text.q: And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you. Go away from me, you who practice lawlessness.’

verse.note: The dismissal closely echoes the Greek version of Psalm 6:8, “Depart from me, all you who practice lawlessness.” Many older translations have “workers of iniquity” or “evildoers”. The Greek word specifically names disregard for God’s law, which sharpens the contrast with doing the Father’s will in verse 21.

text.q: “So everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a sensible man who built his house on rock.

verse.note: Most translations have “wise”. The Greek word is not the usual term for wisdom (σοφός) but one for practical good sense and prudence, the quality of someone who thinks ahead. Standard lexica give “sensible”, “prudent” and “wise” as glosses, so the difference is one of nuance.

text.q: And the rain came down, and the torrents came, and the winds blew and fell upon that house, yet it did not fall, for it had been founded on rock.

verse.note: The word ordinarily means “rivers”. Here it refers to the sudden rush of water that fills dry streambeds in Palestine after heavy rain. Traditional versions have “floods”. “Torrents” keeps the sense of moving streams rather than standing water.

text.q: And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on sand.
And the rain came down, and the torrents came, and the winds blew and battered that house, and it fell—and its fall was great.”

verse.text: When Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astounded at his teaching,
for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not like their scribes.
verse.note: Scribes were trained experts in the Law of Moses who taught and interpreted it, typically by appeal to Scripture and received tradition. The contrast is that Jesus spoke on his own authority, as in the repeated “but I tell you” of this sermon.

verse.text: When he came down from the mountain, large crowds followed him.
And look, a man with a skin disease came up and bowed down before him, saying, “Lord, if you are willing, you can cleanse me.”

note.term: a man with a skin disease

verse.note: The Greek word names someone with the ritually defiling skin condition regulated in Leviticus 13–14, a range of scaly conditions that made a person unclean, which is why the man asks to be “cleansed” and not simply healed. “Leper” today means a person with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the Greek term and may not be included in it. Most translations keep “leper” and explain it in a footnote; scholars widely agree the biblical term is broader.

The verb names the act of prostrating oneself in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it: a god, a king, or a superior from whom one seeks a favor. Here a petitioner approaches Jesus with no confession of divine status, so the gesture itself is rendered. The KJV has “worshipped”; most modern versions have “knelt before him.” Scholars disagree about how much divine recognition Matthew intends in such scenes.

verse.text: And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying, “I am willing. Be cleansed.” And immediately his skin disease was cleansed.
And Jesus said to him, “See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”
verse.note: Leviticus 14 requires a person recovered from such a skin disease to be examined by a priest and to bring offerings before rejoining the community. “Them” may be the priests or the people at large, and the “testimony” may be proof that the man is clean, evidence that Jesus upholds the Law of Moses, or both. The Greek does not settle the question.

verse.text: When he entered Capernaum, a centurion came up to him, begging him
and saying, “Lord, my servant is lying at home paralyzed, terribly tormented.”
verse.note: The Greek word can mean “child,” “boy,” “son” or “servant.” Most translations choose “servant” because the parallel account in Luke 7:2 calls him a slave, but some scholars think Matthew means the centurion’s son. Matthew uses a different word, rendered “slave,” in verse 9.

verse.text: And he said to him, “I will come and cure him.”

note.term: I will come and cure him.
note.traditional: I will come and heal him.

verse.note: The Greek has an emphatic “I” and can equally be read as a question: “Am I to come and cure him?” On that reading Jesus voices a Jew’s hesitation about entering a Gentile’s house, and the centurion’s reply in verse 8 answers the objection. Most translations take it as a statement; a number of commentators prefer the question.

verse.text: But the centurion answered, “Lord, I am not fit to have you come under my roof. But only say the word, and my servant will be healed.
verse.note: The Greek word means “sufficient,” “adequate” or “fit”; it is not the ordinary word for “worthy.” It is the word John the Baptist uses in Matthew 3:11 of his unfitness to carry the coming one’s sandals. Most translations have “worthy” or “I do not deserve.”

text.q: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

verse.text: When Jesus heard this, he was amazed and said to those following him, “Truly I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith.
verse.note: Manuscripts differ here. The reading translated is “with no one in Israel have I found such faith”; many manuscripts read “not even in Israel have I found such faith,” which matches Luke 7:9 and may have been copied from there. The difference is of emphasis more than substance.

text.q: I tell you that many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of the heavens,

verse.note: Matthew’s Greek has the plural, “heavens,” reflecting Hebrew and Aramaic, in which the word is always plural. The phrase is Matthew’s usual equivalent of “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; the plural is kept here as a Semitic turn of phrase a first-century hearer would have noticed.

text.q: but the sons of the kingdom will be thrown out into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

verse.note: “Sons of” something is a Semitic idiom for those who belong to it or stand to inherit it. Here it means those who expected a place by right at the banquet of the age to come, pictured in verse 11 as reclining at a feast with the patriarchs. Some translations paraphrase as “heirs” or “subjects” of the kingdom.

verse.text: And Jesus said to the centurion, “Go. Let it be done for you as you have believed.” And the servant was healed in that very hour.
When Jesus came into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying in bed with a fever.
He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she got up and began to serve him.
When evening came, they brought to him many who were demon-possessed, and he drove out the spirits with a word and cured all who were sick,
so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “He himself took our sicknesses and carried our diseases.”
verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 53:4. Matthew’s wording is closer to the Hebrew than to the Greek Septuagint, which speaks of bearing “sins,” and he applies the line to Jesus’s physical healings.

verse.text: When Jesus saw large crowds around him, he gave orders to go across to the other side.
And a scribe came up and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.”
And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”
Another of the disciples said to him, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.”
But Jesus said to him, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.”

note.term: leave the dead to bury their own dead

verse.note: Burying a parent was among the most binding family duties in Jewish society and in the ancient world generally, so the saying is deliberately shocking. The “dead” who are to do the burying are usually understood as those who are not alive to the kingdom. Some interpreters think the father had not yet died and the man was asking to stay home until he did, but this is disputed.

verse.text: When he got into a boat, his disciples followed him.
And look, a great storm arose on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was sleeping.
verse.note: The Greek word means “a shaking” and ordinarily refers to an earthquake; Matthew uses it that way at Jesus’s death and resurrection (27:54; 28:2). Used of the sea it denotes a violent storm, and the parallel accounts in Mark and Luke use a word for a windstorm. The “great storm” is answered by the “great calm” of verse 26.

verse.text: They came and woke him, saying, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!”
And he said to them, “Why are you such cowards, you of little faith?” Then he got up and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.
verse.note: The Greek adjective means “cowardly” or “timid” and is a term of reproach, stronger than the ordinary vocabulary for fear. Most translations soften it to “afraid” or “fearful.”

verse.text: The people were amazed, saying, “What kind of person is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him?”
When he came to the other side, to the region of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs. They were so fierce that no one was able to pass along that road.
verse.note: Manuscripts vary among “Gadarenes,” “Gerasenes” and “Gergesenes,” both here and in the parallel accounts in Mark 5:1 and Luke 8:26. “Gadarenes” is the best-supported reading in Matthew; Gadara was a city of the Decapolis some miles southeast of the lake whose territory seems to have reached the shore. The KJV, following later manuscripts, has “Gergesenes.”

verse.text: And look, they cried out, saying, “What do you want with us, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us?”
Now at a distance from them a large herd of pigs was feeding.
The demons begged him, saying, “If you drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.”
And he said to them, “Go!” So they came out and went off into the pigs, and look, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and died in the waters.
Those tending them fled, went off into the town, and reported everything, including what had happened to the demon-possessed men.
And look, the whole town came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him they begged him to leave their region.
He got into a boat, crossed over, and came to his own town.
verse.note: This is Capernaum, where Jesus had settled according to Matthew 4:13, not Nazareth where he grew up. Mark’s parallel account names the town.

verse.text: And look, some people were bringing him a paralyzed man lying on a bed. Seeing their faith, Jesus said to the paralyzed man, “Take courage, child; your sins are forgiven.”
And look, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.”
Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said, “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?
verse.note: The SBLGNT reads “knowing.” Many manuscripts, followed by some other critical editions, have a very similar-looking Greek word meaning “seeing.” The sense is little affected either way.

text.q: For which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?

verse.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” then he said to the paralyzed man, “Get up, pick up your bed, and go to your house.”
And he got up and went off to his house.
When the crowds saw it, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to people.
As Jesus went on from there, he saw a man named Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
verse.note: This was a station where tolls and customs duties on goods were collected. The collectors worked under contract for the ruling authorities and were widely despised as dishonest and as collaborators. That is why “tax collectors and sinners” are paired in the verses that follow.

verse.text: And as he was reclining at table in the house, look, many tax collectors and sinners came and reclined with Jesus and his disciples.
When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
But when he heard it, he said, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.

text.q: Go and learn what this means: ‘I want mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous but sinners.”

note.term: I want mercy and not sacrifice
note.traditional: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice

verse.note: Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6. In its original setting the saying is generally understood as a statement of priority rather than a rejection of the sacrificial system: loyal kindness matters more to God than ritual. Matthew has Jesus quote the same line again at 12:7.

verse.text: Then John’s disciples came to him and said, “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?”
Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “sons of the bridal chamber,” a Semitic idiom for those who belong to the wedding party. It may mean the guests in general or more narrowly the bridegroom’s attendants. Most modern translations render it “wedding guests.”

text.q: No one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch pulls away from the garment, and a worse tear results.
Nor do people put new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the skins burst, the wine pours out, and the skins are ruined. Instead, they put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.”

verse.text: While he was saying these things to them, look, an official came and bowed down before him, saying, “My daughter has just died. But come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.”
verse.note: The Greek word covers anyone holding a position of authority, from a magistrate to a local community leader, whereas “ruler” now suggests a sovereign. Mark and Luke identify the man as Jairus, a leader of the synagogue. The same Greek word is used in verse 34, where “ruler” of the demons fits the sense.

The Greek verb names the act of prostrating oneself in reverence, and its meaning depends on who receives it. Here a petitioner falls before Jesus to beg for help, and the scene contains no confession of divine status, so the gesture is translated rather than “worshiped.” Most modern versions do likewise (“knelt before him”), though scholars differ on how much recognition of Jesus Matthew intends in such scenes.

verse.text: And Jesus got up and followed him, and so did his disciples.
And look, a woman who had been suffering from bleeding for twelve years came up behind him and touched the tassel of his cloak,
verse.note: The word can mean simply the edge of a garment. It is also the Septuagint’s term for the tassels that Jewish men wore on the corners of their cloaks in obedience to Numbers 15:38–39, and Matthew uses it in that sense at 23:5. Many scholars think the tassel is meant here, though “edge” remains possible.

verse.text: for she was saying to herself, “If I only touch his cloak, I will be made well.”
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for rescuing someone from danger or illness, and it is the same verb translated “save” elsewhere in the New Testament. It occurs three times in verses 21–22. Physical healing is in view here, but the link Jesus makes with faith may have suggested the wider sense to Matthew’s readers as well.

verse.text: Jesus turned and saw her, and he said, “Take courage, daughter; your faith has made you well.” And the woman was made well from that hour.
When Jesus came to the official’s house and saw the flute players and the crowd in an uproar,
he said, “Go away, for the girl has not died but is sleeping.” And they laughed at him.
But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl got up.
verse.note: The Greek verb is passive in form and can mean either “got up” or “was raised.” It is also the usual New Testament verb for raising the dead. It is used of the paralyzed man in verses 5–7 and is rendered “got up” throughout the chapter, but “was raised” is equally possible here.

verse.text: And this report went out into that whole region.
As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”
When he had gone into the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.”
Then he touched their eyes and said, “Let it be done for you according to your faith.”
And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, “See that no one knows about this.”
But they went out and spread the news about him throughout that whole region.
As they were going out, look, people brought to him a mute man who was possessed by a demon.
And when the demon had been driven out, the mute man spoke. The crowds were amazed and said, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel!”
But the Pharisees said, “It is by the ruler of the demons that he drives out demons.”

note.term: It is by the ruler of the demons that he drives out demons

verse.note: This verse is missing from a few witnesses, including Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts, and some scholars suspect it was brought in from the similar charge at 12:24. The great majority of manuscripts include it, and the SBLGNT prints it without brackets.

verse.text: And Jesus went around all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness.
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, and was also used of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term and a book title, which hides that everyday sense. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

verse.text: When he saw the crowds, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.

text.q: So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.”

verse.text: And calling his twelve disciples to him, he gave them authority over unclean spirits, to drive them out and to heal every disease and every illness.
These are the names of the twelve apostles: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus;
Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, the one who also handed him over.

note.traditional: the Canaanite; the Cananaean; the Zealot

verse.note: The byname transliterates an Aramaic word meaning “zealous one”; it has nothing to do with Canaan or the village of Cana. Luke’s list gives the Greek equivalent, “the Zealot”. Whether it marks religious zeal in general or a link with a militant movement is disputed.

The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing a person into someone else’s custody, and the same word is used in verses 17, 19 and 21 for what will happen to the disciples. Most English versions say “betrayed” when Judas is the subject, which names the treachery the story supplies but hides the repetition. Some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual sense here.

verse.text: These twelve Jesus sent out with these instructions: “Do not go off down any road to the Gentiles, and do not enter any town of the Samaritans;
verse.note: One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural from a Jewish standpoint, the non-Jewish peoples; it is rendered “Gentiles” or “nations” according to sense. The phrase is literally “a road of Gentiles”, most likely a road leading into Gentile territory. This mission is limited to Israel; the Gospel’s closing scene sends the disciples to all the nations.

text.q: but go instead to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
As you go, proclaim, ‘The kingdom of the heavens has come near.’

verse.note: The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. The phrase is Matthew’s usual equivalent of “the kingdom of God”.

text.q: Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse those with skin disease, drive out demons. You received without payment; give without payment.

verse.note: The word names people with the scaly skin conditions regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which made a person ritually unclean; that is why they are “cleansed” and not simply healed. “Leper” today means someone with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the Greek term and may not even be included in it. Most translations keep “lepers” with a footnote, partly because “skin disease” can understate the social exclusion involved.

text.q: Do not acquire gold or silver or copper for your belts,
nor a bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff; for the worker is worthy of his food.
Whatever town or village you enter, find out who in it is worthy, and stay there until you leave.
As you enter the house, greet it.
If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.

note.term: let your peace come upon it

verse.note: The ordinary Jewish greeting on entering a house was a wish of peace, so “greet it” in verse 12 means to speak peace over the household. The saying treats that spoken peace as a real blessing that either rests on the house or returns to the one who gave it.

text.q: And if anyone will not welcome you or listen to your words, shake the dust off your feet as you leave that house or town.
Truly I tell you, it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.
Look, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves; so be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.
Be on your guard against people, for they will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues,
and you will be brought before governors and kings on my account, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles.
But when they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour.
For it is not you who are speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you.
Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his child; children will rise up against parents and have them put to death.
You will be hated by everyone because of my name. But whoever endures to the end will be saved.
When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next; for truly I tell you, you will certainly not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.

note.term: before the Son of Man comes

verse.note: What “coming” is meant is disputed. Proposals include Jesus’ vindication in his resurrection and exaltation, the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, and his final coming, with the mission to Israel continuing until then. The Greek does not settle the question.

text.q: A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above his master.

verse.note: The Greek word means a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Many English versions soften it to “servant”; some recent ones use “slave”, as here.

text.q: It is enough for the disciple to become like his teacher, and the slave like his master. If they have called the head of the house Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!

verse.note: A name for the ruler of the demons, as the accusation later in this Gospel makes explicit. Its origin is uncertain; many scholars think it means something like “lord of the dwelling”, which would make a pun with “head of the house”. Older English versions have “Beelzebub”, following the Latin.

text.q: So do not fear them; for nothing is covered that will not be uncovered, and nothing hidden that will not be made known.
What I tell you in the dark, say in the light; and what you hear in your ear, proclaim on the housetops.
And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Fear instead the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the name for the place of final judgment. “Hell” merges it with Hades and with later imagery, so the name is kept. Many translations still use “hell”, usually with a footnote giving Gehenna.

text.q: Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.

verse.note: The coin is an assarion, a small copper coin worth one-sixteenth of a denarius, the denarius being roughly a day’s wage for a laborer. “Penny” stands for a coin of very little value.
The Greek says only “without your Father”. Translations often supply “without your Father’s will”, “knowledge” or “care”; the Greek does not choose among them, and the rendering leaves it open.

text.q: As for you, even the hairs of your head are all numbered.
So do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows.
So everyone who acknowledges me before people, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in the heavens;
but whoever denies me before people, I also will deny before my Father who is in the heavens.
Do not think that I came to bring peace on the earth. I did not come to bring peace, but a sword.
For I came to turn a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law;

note.term: to turn a man against his father

verse.note: Verses 35–36 echo Micah 7:6, where the breakdown of trust within the family is a sign of a time of crisis. Jesus applies the prophet’s words to the division his own mission will cause.

text.q: and a person’s enemies will be the members of their own household.
Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me;
and whoever does not take up their cross and follow after me is not worthy of me.
Whoever finds their life will lose it, and whoever loses their life on my account will find it.

verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one rendered “soul” in verse 28. It most often means a person’s life or living self; “soul” is used in verse 28 because there it is set against the body as what killing cannot reach. All major translations divide the word between “life” and “soul” by context.

text.q: Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
Whoever welcomes a prophet as a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever welcomes a righteous person as a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.

note.traditional: in the name of a prophet

verse.note: The Greek is literally “into the name of a prophet”, an idiom meaning “on the ground that he is a prophet”. The literal phrase suggests to an English reader that someone’s name is being invoked, so the sense is given instead; several modern versions do the same. In verse 42 “as a disciple” likewise means that the little one is given the drink because he is a disciple.
