text.q: And whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water as a disciple—truly I tell you, that person will certainly not lose their reward.”

verse.text: When Jesus had finished giving instructions to his twelve disciples, he moved on from there to teach and proclaim in their towns.
Now when John heard in prison about the works of the Messiah, he sent word through his disciples
verse.note: The Greek has the article (“the Christ”) and uses the word as a title for the anointed king Israel expected, not as a name. “Messiah” conveys that title to a modern reader, and several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. “Christ” is kept where the word works as part of Jesus’ name.

verse.text: and said to him, “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect someone else?”
Jesus answered them, “Go and report to John what you hear and see:

text.q: the blind see again and the lame walk, those with skin disease are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised and the poor are brought good news.

verse.note: The Greek word names people with the scaly skin conditions regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which made a person ritually unclean; this is why they are “cleansed” and not simply healed. “Leper” today means someone with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the biblical term and may not be included in it. Most translations keep “lepers” with a footnote; the conditions involved were serious and brought social exclusion.

note.term: the poor are brought good news
note.traditional: the poor have the gospel preached to them

verse.note: Jesus’ answer is a chain of phrases from Isaiah’s pictures of God’s coming restoration (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1; compare 26:19). He does not answer John’s question directly but points to what is happening and leaves John to draw the conclusion. The verb is the ordinary Greek word for announcing good news, traditionally rendered “preach the gospel.”

text.q: And blessed is anyone who does not stumble because of me.”

note.traditional: be offended in me; take offense at me

verse.note: The verb comes from a word for a trap or obstacle and means to be tripped up in one’s trust or loyalty. “Offended” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak. Modern versions are divided here between “takes no offense at me” and “does not stumble on account of me.”

verse.text: As they were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?

text.q: Then what did you go out to see? Someone dressed in soft clothing? Look, those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings.
Then why did you go out? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Look, I am sending my messenger ahead of you, who will prepare your way before you.’

verse.note: The quotation follows Malachi 3:1, with wording that also recalls Exodus 23:20. The Greek word for “messenger” is the same one usually rendered “angel”; here it refers to a human herald.

text.q: Truly I tell you, among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen; yet the least in the kingdom of the heavens is greater than he.

verse.note: Matthew’s characteristic phrase has “heavens” in the plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The meaning is the same as “the kingdom of God” in the other Gospels.

text.q: From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of the heavens has been suffering violence, and the violent are seizing it.

verse.note: The Greek verb can be read as passive (“suffers violence”) or as middle (“advances forcefully”), and this is one of the most disputed sayings in the Gospels. The passive is taken here, with “the violent” understood as hostile, which fits John’s imprisonment. Others read the saying positively, of eager people pressing into the kingdom (compare Luke 16:16).

text.q: For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John,
and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah, who is to come.

note.term: he is Elijah, who is to come

verse.note: Malachi 4:5 (3:23 in the Hebrew numbering) promises that Elijah will be sent before the day of the Lord, and many expected his return ahead of God’s decisive intervention. Jesus identifies John as the one who fills that role.

text.q: Let anyone who has ears hear.
To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces who call out to the others
and say, ‘We played the pipe for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’
For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her works.”

verse.note: The verb belongs to the word-family that English divides between “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” “justify.” Here it means to be shown to be in the right, which “vindicated” says more plainly than “justified.” Many modern translations render it the same way.

Many manuscripts read “children” in place of “works,” matching the parallel in Luke 7:35. “Works” has early support and is preferred by most editors, since copyists would more likely have altered Matthew to match Luke than the reverse. It also ties back to “the works of the Messiah” in verse 2.

verse.text: Then he began to reproach the towns in which most of his deeds of power had been done, because they had not turned back:
verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used in the plural for acts that display it. There is no dispute about the meaning; “miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering. “Deeds of power” is chosen so that the link with the word “power” elsewhere stays visible.

“Repent” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have turned back long ago in sackcloth and ashes.
But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.
And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? You will go down to Hades. For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day.

note.term: You will go down to Hades

verse.note: The taunt echoes Isaiah 14:13–15, addressed to the king of Babylon, who aimed to ascend to heaven and was brought down to the realm of the dead. Hades here is that realm, the lowest place as heaven is the highest, and is distinct from the place of final punishment. Some manuscripts read “you will be brought down.”

text.q: But I tell you that it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”

verse.text: At that time Jesus said, “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to infants.

text.q: Yes, Father, for this was what pleased you.
All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.
Come to me, all you who toil and are burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.

verse.note: “Meek” now suggests weakness, which the Greek word does not; it describes someone who is not harsh or self-assertive. “Gentle” or “humble” is the mainstream modern rendering.
A yoke was a familiar Jewish image for submitting to instruction, used of wisdom’s teaching (as in Sirach 51:26) and of the Law. “You will find rest for your souls” echoes Jeremiah 6:16.

text.q: For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.”

verse.text: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and eat.
But when the Pharisees saw this, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not permitted on the Sabbath.”
verse.note: The Greek verb means simply “it is allowed” and contains no word for law, though the standard in view is the Law of Moses as the Pharisees applied it. Most translations have “lawful.” Plucking grain by hand in someone else’s field was itself allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25); the objection is that doing so on the Sabbath counted as reaping, a form of work.

verse.text: He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he and those with him were hungry—

text.q: how he entered the house of God and they ate the loaves of presentation, which neither he nor those with him were permitted to eat, but only the priests?

note.traditional: the bread of the Presence; the showbread

verse.note: The Greek phrase means loaves “set out” or “presented” before God: twelve loaves laid on a table in the sanctuary each Sabbath and afterward eaten only by the priests (Leviticus 24:5–9). The usual rendering, “bread of the Presence,” translates the Hebrew expression behind the phrase, not the Greek. The story of David is told in 1 Samuel 21:1–6.

text.q: Or have you not read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and yet are guiltless?
But I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.

verse.note: The Greek adjective is neuter, “something greater,” not masculine, “someone greater,” and the same is true of the parallel sayings in verses 41 and 42. Some translations nevertheless render “one greater.” The neuter may be an indirect way of pointing to Jesus himself, or it may refer to what is happening through him.

text.q: If you had known what this means—‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’—you would not have condemned the guiltless.
For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”

verse.text: Moving on from there, he went into their synagogue.
And there was a man with a withered hand. They questioned him, “Is it permitted to heal on the Sabbath?” They asked this so that they might accuse him.
He said to them, “Which of you, if he has one sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out?

text.q: How much more valuable, then, is a person than a sheep! So it is permitted to do good on the Sabbath.”

verse.text: Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and it was restored, as sound as the other.
But the Pharisees went out and plotted against him, to destroy him.
But Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. Many followed him, and he healed them all,
and he sternly warned them not to make him known,
so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:

text.q: “Here is my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul delights. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles.

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 42:1–4, in a form that matches neither the Hebrew nor the Septuagint exactly. The Greek word can mean either “servant” or “child.” Isaiah’s Hebrew means “servant,” and that is the usual rendering here, though the wording “my beloved, in whom my soul delights” also recalls the voice at Jesus’ baptism.

One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples as distinct from Israel; English has to choose. “Gentiles” is the usual rendering here and in verse 21, and “nations” would be equally possible.

The Greek word covers both “judgment” and “justice.” In the Isaiah quotation it stands for a Hebrew word for the right order God establishes, so “justice” is used here and in verse 20. In verses 36, 41 and 42 the same Greek word is rendered “judgment.”

text.q: He will not quarrel or shout, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.
A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not put out, until he brings justice through to victory.
And in his name the Gentiles will hope.”

verse.text: Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the mute man could speak and see.
All the crowds were amazed and said, “Could this perhaps be the Son of David?”
But when the Pharisees heard this, they said, “This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons.”
verse.note: A name for the chief of the demons, identified with Satan in verse 26. Its origin is disputed; it is often connected with the Philistine god called Baal-zebub in 2 Kings 1. The spelling “Beelzebub” in older English Bibles comes from the Latin tradition, not from the Greek manuscripts.

verse.text: Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or household divided against itself will stand.

text.q: And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand?
And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? For this reason they themselves will be your judges.

verse.note: In Semitic idiom “sons” can mean the members of a group, so the phrase refers to people of the Pharisees’ own circle, such as their pupils, who also practiced exorcism. The argument is that the accusation against Jesus would condemn them as well.

text.q: But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
Or how can anyone enter the strong man’s house and carry off his goods unless he first ties up the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
For this reason I tell you, people will be forgiven every sin and blasphemy, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.
Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the one to come.
Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit.
Offspring of vipers! How can you speak good things when you are evil? For the mouth speaks from the overflow of the heart.
The good person brings good things out of his good storehouse, and the evil person brings evil things out of his evil storehouse.
I tell you that people will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they speak.
For by your words you will be vindicated, and by your words you will be condemned.”

verse.note: This is the verb traditionally rendered “justified.” In a courtroom setting such as this one it means to be declared in the right, the opposite of being condemned, and some translations have “acquitted.” Greek uses a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify).

verse.text: Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from you.”
But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation demands a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet.
verse.note: The prophets pictured Israel’s unfaithfulness to God as a wife’s adultery against her husband, as in Hosea, Jeremiah 3 and Ezekiel 16. The word here charges the generation with unfaithfulness to God, not with sexual sin.

text.q: For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes any huge sea creature and is the word the Septuagint uses in Jonah, where the Hebrew has “a great fish.” “Whale” is too specific. Some modern translations also have “sea monster”; others have “great fish” or “huge fish,” following the Hebrew of Jonah.

text.q: The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they turned back at the preaching of Jonah—and look, something greater than Jonah is here.

verse.note: “Repent” now suggests mainly feeling sorry, whereas the Greek verb carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. In Jonah 3 the Ninevites “turned from their evil way.” Most translations keep “repented” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: The queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon—and look, something greater than Solomon is here.
When the unclean spirit goes out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest and does not find it.
Then it says, ‘I will return to my house that I came out of.’ And when it arrives, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order.

Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they go in and live there, and that person’s final condition becomes worse than the first. So it will be for this evil generation as well.”

verse.text: While he was still speaking to the crowds, his mother and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak to him.
Someone said to him, “Look, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you.”
verse.note: Some important early manuscripts lack this verse. It was probably dropped by accident, since it ends with the same Greek word as verse 46 and verse 48 presupposes it. Some editions of the Greek text print it in brackets.

verse.text: But he replied to the one who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?”
And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers!

text.q: For whoever does the will of my Father in the heavens is my brother and sister and mother.”

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.”

verse.text: On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea.
Large crowds gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat down, while the whole crowd stood on the shore.
And he told them many things in parables, saying, “Look! A sower went out to sow.

text.q: As he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and ate them up.
Others fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and they sprang up immediately because the soil had no depth,
but when the sun rose they were scorched, and because they had no root they withered.
Others fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked them.
Others fell on the good soil and produced a crop—some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
Let the one who has ears hear.”

verse.text: Then the disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?”
He answered them, “Because to you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of the heavens, but to them it has not been given.
verse.note: Most English versions have “mysteries.” In Jewish Greek of the period this was the ordinary word for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose, whereas English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding. Lexicons give “secret” as a primary gloss, and several mainstream versions use it in this saying, though many scholars defend “mystery” as an established technical term.

Matthew’s Greek is plural here, as it is every time he uses this phrase, reflecting a Semitic way of speaking about God’s dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; the plural is kept because a first-century hearer would have noticed it. The meaning is the same as “kingdom of God” in the other Gospels.

text.q: For whoever has will be given more and will have an abundance; but whoever does not have, even what they have will be taken away from them.
This is why I speak to them in parables: because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand.
In them the prophecy of Isaiah is being fulfilled, which says: ‘You will hear and hear but never understand; you will look and look but never see.

For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they have barely heard, and they have shut their eyes; otherwise they might see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.’
But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.
For truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.
You, then, hear the parable of the sower.
When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in that person’s heart. This is the one sown along the path.
As for the one sown on the rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy,
but has no root within and lasts only a short time; when affliction or persecution comes because of the word, such a person immediately falls away.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “tribulation,” which many readers now hear as the name of a specific end-time period. The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that bears down on someone. Lexicons agree on the sense, and English versions vary among “tribulation,” “affliction,” “trouble” and “distress.”

The King James Version has “is offended,” which now suggests hurt feelings. The verb means to be tripped up so as to abandon one’s loyalty, and most modern versions also render it “falls away” here. The same verb appears in verse 57, where the sense is that people were affronted by Jesus, and it is translated “took offense” there.

text.q: As for the one sown among the thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the worry of this age and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.

verse.note: Many versions have “the cares of the world” or “the worries of this life.” The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, and it reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. It is the same word used in “the end of the age” in verses 39, 40 and 49, and a different word from the one translated “world” in verse 38.

text.q: As for the one sown on the good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and yields—one a hundredfold, another sixty, another thirty.”

verse.text: He set another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of the heavens may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field.

text.q: But while people were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away.

verse.note: The Greek word names a particular weed, generally identified as darnel, a grass that looks very much like wheat until the ears form. That is why the weeds only become apparent when the crop appears (verse 26), and why pulling them early risks uprooting the wheat. Older versions call them “tares.”

text.q: When the plants sprouted and produced a crop, then the weeds appeared as well.
The householder’s slaves came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?’

verse.note: Most English versions have “servants.” The Greek word ordinarily meant a slave, a person owned by the householder, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. “Servant” suggests a hired employee, which is a different Greek word.

text.q: He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ The slaves said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and collect them?’
But he said, ‘No, for in collecting the weeds you might uproot the wheat along with them.
Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, “Collect the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”

verse.text: He set another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of the heavens is like a mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field.

text.q: It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the sky come and nest in its branches.”

verse.text: He told them another parable: “The kingdom of the heavens is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.”
verse.note: The measure named here was a dry measure usually estimated at around thirteen liters, so three of them is a very large batch of flour—enough bread to feed well over a hundred people. The exact size is uncertain, but the point of the picture is that a small amount of leaven works through a huge quantity of dough.

verse.text: Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and he said nothing to them without a parable,
so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation.”

note.traditional: from the foundation of the world

verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 78:2. Many manuscripts read “from the foundation of the world”; the Greek text translated here has the shorter reading without “of the world,” though the meaning is the same. A few manuscripts also read “through the prophet Isaiah,” which is probably a copyist’s slip, since the words are not from Isaiah.

verse.text: Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.”
He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.

text.q: The field is the world, and the good seed—these are the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one,
and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
So just as the weeds are collected and burned with fire, so it will be at the end of the age.
The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will collect out of his kingdom everything that causes stumbling and those who practice lawlessness,

verse.note: The King James Version has “all things that offend”; modern versions have “all causes of sin” or “everything that causes sin.” The Greek word means a trap or obstacle that makes someone fall, and figuratively whatever leads a person into sin or ruin. Here the collective may include people as well as things.

text.q: and they will throw them into the furnace of fire. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Let the one who has ears hear.
The kingdom of the heavens is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and hid; and in his joy he goes and sells everything he has and buys that field.
Again, the kingdom of the heavens is like a merchant searching for fine pearls.
When he found one pearl of great value, he went away and sold everything he had and bought it.
Again, the kingdom of the heavens is like a dragnet that was cast into the sea and gathered fish of every kind.
When it was full, they hauled it up onto the shore, sat down, and collected the good ones into containers, but threw the bad ones out.
So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will go out and separate the evil from among the righteous
and throw them into the furnace of fire. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

verse.text: Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.”
And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been made a disciple for the kingdom of the heavens is like a householder who brings out of his storeroom things new and old.”

note.term: made a disciple for the kingdom of the heavens
note.traditional: instructed unto the kingdom of heaven

verse.note: The Greek verb can mean either “become a disciple” or “be instructed,” and the kingdom may be that for which, or about which, the scribe is trained. Versions accordingly vary between “trained for the kingdom,” “instructed about the kingdom” and “become a disciple of the kingdom.” The rendering here keeps the link with the word “disciple,” which the Greek makes audible.

verse.text: When Jesus had finished these parables, he moved on from there.
Coming to his hometown, he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these deeds of power?
verse.note: Traditional renderings are “mighty works” or “miracles.” The Greek is simply the ordinary word for power, used in the plural for acts that display it, and “deeds of power” keeps that connection visible. There is no dispute about the meaning, and “miracles” is an equally acceptable translation.

text.q: Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is his mother not called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?
And are not all his sisters here with us? Where then did this man get all these things?”

verse.text: And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.”
And he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.
At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus,
verse.note: This is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome. “Tetrarch” was the title of a dependent ruler ranking below a king. Matthew calls him “the king” in verse 9, which reflects popular usage and not his official rank.

verse.text: and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead, and that is why these powers are at work in him.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary word for power. In the plural it often means miracles, which is how the KJV takes it here (“mighty works do shew forth themselves in him”). Because these are said to be “at work in him,” most modern versions understand forces operating through Jesus rather than the deeds themselves, and the translation follows that reading.

verse.text: For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him away in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip,
because John had been telling him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.”

note.term: It is not lawful for you to have her

verse.note: Herodias had left her first husband, Antipas’s half-brother, to marry Antipas. The Law of Moses forbade a man to marry his brother’s wife while the brother was alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). The Greek verb tense indicates that John said this repeatedly.

verse.text: Though he wanted to kill him, he was afraid of the crowd, because they held him to be a prophet.
But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced in front of the company and pleased Herod,
so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she asked.
Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me here, on a platter, the head of John the Baptist.”
The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his dinner guests he ordered it to be given,
and he sent and had John beheaded in the prison.
His head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother.
His disciples came, took away the corpse, and buried him; then they went and told Jesus.
When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there by boat to a deserted place by himself. But the crowds heard of it and followed him on foot from the towns.
When he came ashore he saw a large crowd, and he was moved with compassion for them and healed their sick.

When evening came, the disciples approached him and said, “This is a deserted place, and the hour is already late. Send the crowds away, so that they can go into the villages and buy themselves food.”
But Jesus said to them, “They do not need to go away. You give them something to eat.”
They said to him, “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.”
He said, “Bring them here to me.”

Then he ordered the crowds to recline on the grass. Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing; then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
verse.note: The Greek verb has no stated object, so it can be read as blessing the food or as blessing God. In Jewish practice the prayer before a meal blessed God for the food, and that is the more likely sense here. “Said a blessing” leaves the object open as the Greek does.

verse.text: They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces—twelve baskets full.
Those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the crowds away.
After sending the crowds away, he went up the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.
The boat was already a long way from the land, battered by the waves, for the wind was against it.

note.traditional: many furlongs / in the midst of the sea

verse.note: The Greek says “many stadia”; a stadion was about 185 meters or 600 feet, so the boat was well out on the lake. Many manuscripts read instead “in the middle of the sea,” as in Mark 6:47, and the KJV follows that reading.

verse.text: In the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.

note.term: the fourth watch of the night

verse.note: The Roman system divided the night into four watches. The fourth was the last, running from roughly three to six in the morning, so the disciples had been struggling against the wind for most of the night.

verse.text: When the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified and said, “It is a ghost!” And they cried out in fear.
But at once Jesus spoke to them: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally “I am,” the normal way to say “It’s me.” The same words are also God’s self-identification in the Greek Old Testament (for example Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10). Many scholars think Matthew intends that echo here, in a scene where Jesus walks on the sea and is then worshiped; others take it as simple self-identification.

verse.text: Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.”
He said, “Come.” So Peter got down out of the boat, walked on the water, and came toward Jesus.
But when he saw the strong wind, he became afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me!”
verse.note: A few important early manuscripts lack the word “strong” and read simply “when he saw the wind.” Editors are divided on whether the word is original, but the sense is little affected.

verse.text: Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
And when they got into the boat, the wind died down.
Those in the boat worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.”
verse.note: The Greek has no definite article and could be rendered “God’s Son” or, less probably, “a son of God.” Greek often leaves out the article before a noun in this position, and Matthew’s later use of the title (16:16; 27:54) supports the definite sense adopted here and in most translations.

verse.text: When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret.
The men of that place recognized him and sent word throughout that whole surrounding region, and people brought to him all who were sick,
and they begged him to let them just touch the tassel of his cloak; and all who touched it were made completely well.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean the edge of a garment. It is also the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the tassels that Israelite men were commanded to wear on the corners of their cloaks as a reminder of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–39). Matthew uses it in that sense at 23:5, and it most likely means the same here. Most translations have “fringe” or “hem.”

verse.text: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said,

text.q: “Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

verse.note: This was the body of rulings handed down by earlier teachers, which the Pharisees treated as binding alongside the written Law. The handwashing at issue was a ritual rinsing for purity, not hygiene, and the Law of Moses does not require it of ordinary people before meals. “Eat bread” is a Semitic idiom for having a meal.

verse.text: He answered them, “And why do you yourselves break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?

text.q: For God said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever speaks evil of father or mother must be put to death.’
But you say, ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “Whatever benefit you might have had from me is a gift to God,”

verse.note: The Greek has only “gift,” the Septuagint’s regular word for an offering to God; the parallel in Mark 7:11 gives the Hebrew term, korban. Declaring property an offering placed it under a vow, so that it could no longer be used to support one’s parents. The ruling that such a person “is not to honor his father” can be read either as forbidding the support or as releasing him from the duty.

text.q: is not to honor his father.’ So you have nullified the word of God for the sake of your tradition.

verse.note: Manuscripts divide here between “the word,” “the law,” and “the commandment” of God; the sense is hardly affected. Many manuscripts also add “or his mother” after “his father.”

text.q: Hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied rightly about you when he said,
‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me;
in vain they worship me, teaching human precepts as doctrines.’”

verse.text: Then he called the crowd to him and said to them, “Listen and understand:

text.q: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth—that defiles a person.”

verse.note: The verb literally means “make common,” that is, ritually impure and unfit for contact with what is holy. The argument throughout is about purity before God, not cleanliness, which is why the saying shocked the Pharisees.

verse.text: Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees took offense when they heard this saying?”
He answered, “Every plant that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.

text.q: Leave them be; they are blind guides of the blind. And if one blind person guides another, both will fall into a pit.”

verse.text: Peter said to him in response, “Explain this parable to us.”
He said, “Are even you still without understanding?

text.q: Do you not see that everything that goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine?

note.traditional: is expelled; goes out into the sewer

verse.note: The Greek names the place plainly: a privy or latrine. Many English versions soften this to “is expelled” or “out of the body,” and the King James has “the draught.” The bluntness is part of the argument, since food simply passes through and never reaches the heart.

text.q: But what comes out of the mouth comes from the heart, and that is what defiles a person.
For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, slander.

verse.note: The Greek word covers abusive speech against people (slander) and against God (blasphemy). The list follows the order of the commandments concerning one’s neighbor and the word comes right after false testimony, so most modern versions take it as slander. Speech against God cannot be ruled out.

text.q: These are the things that defile a person; but eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person.”

verse.text: Jesus left there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon.
Just then a Canaanite woman from that region came out and kept crying out, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely tormented by a demon.”
verse.note: Mark 7:26 describes the woman as a Greek of Syrophoenician origin. “Canaanite” was by this time an old-fashioned, biblical term, recalling the peoples Israel displaced from the land. It sharpens the contrast with her address to Jesus as “Son of David.”

verse.text: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and kept asking him, “Send her away, because she keeps crying out behind us.”
verse.note: The disciples may simply want her dismissed, or they may mean “give her what she wants so that she will go.” Jesus’ reply, which explains why he is not helping her, fits the second reading better. The Greek verb itself says only “send away” or “release.”

verse.text: He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
But she came and bowed down before him, saying, “Lord, help me!”
verse.note: The Greek verb names the act of prostrating oneself, and its significance depends on who receives it and why. Here a petitioner throws herself down before Jesus to plead for help, and modern “worship” would claim more than the scene states. Most modern versions render similarly (“knelt before him”), though scholars disagree about how much recognition of Jesus’ divine status Matthew intends in such scenes.

verse.text: He answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
verse.note: The Greek word is a diminutive form, which may mean small dogs or house dogs as distinct from street scavengers; the picture of dogs under the family table supports this. Some scholars think the diminutive had lost its force by this period. Either way, “dogs” was a known Jewish term of contempt for Gentiles, and the saying is harsh on its face.

verse.text: She said, “Yes, Lord, for even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”
verse.note: Most English versions have the woman object: “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs...” The Greek connective means “for indeed” or “for even,” not “yet.” She accepts the image and argues from within it: the dogs do get fed, from what falls from the same table.

verse.text: Then Jesus answered her, “Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed from that very hour.
Jesus moved on from there and came beside the Sea of Galilee, and he went up the mountain and sat down there.
Large crowds came to him, bringing with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the crippled, and many others. They laid them at his feet, and he healed them,
so that the crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled made whole, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.

Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I feel compassion for the crowd, because they have stayed with me three days now and have nothing to eat. I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may collapse on the way.”
The disciples said to him, “Where in a remote place could we get enough loaves to satisfy so large a crowd?”
Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.”
After directing the crowd to recline on the ground,
he took the seven loaves and the fish, gave thanks, broke them, and kept giving them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven baskets full.
Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.
After sending the crowds away, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read Magadan, a place otherwise unknown; later manuscripts replace it with the familiar Magdala, which the King James follows. The parallel in Mark 8:10 has Dalmanutha, also unidentified.

verse.text: The Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven.
verse.note: The older English tradition has “tempting,” but the Greek verb means to put someone to the test, here with hostile intent. Modern English “tempt” has narrowed to enticing someone to sin, which is not the point. Most modern translations also use “test” in this verse.

verse.text: He answered them, “When evening comes, you say, ‘Fair weather, for the sky is red,’
verse.note: The weather saying, from these words to the end of verse 3, is absent from several important early manuscripts, and some scholars think it was added later under the influence of Luke 12:54–56. Others think it is original and was dropped by copyists in regions such as Egypt, where a red morning sky does not signal rain. The edition translated here prints the words without brackets.

text.q: and in the morning, ‘Stormy today, for the sky is red and overcast.’ You know how to interpret the face of the sky, but the signs of the times you cannot.

verse.text: An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” And he left them and went away.
verse.note: Jesus has already explained this phrase at 12:39–40, where Jonah’s three days in the sea creature point to the Son of Man’s three days in the earth. “Adulterous” follows the prophets’ image of Israel’s unfaithfulness to God as marital infidelity. It is not a charge of sexual misconduct.

verse.text: When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring bread.
Jesus said to them, “Watch out, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”
They began discussing this among themselves, saying, “We didn’t bring any bread.”
Aware of this, Jesus said, “You of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves that you brought no bread?

text.q: Do you not yet understand? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?
Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many large baskets you gathered?
How do you not understand that I was not speaking to you about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

verse.text: Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven in bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?”
They said, “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and still others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.”
He said to them, “But you—who do you say I am?”
Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one,” the king Israel was expecting. Here it is a title under discussion, not a name, so “Messiah” conveys what Peter’s hearers would have understood. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it works as a name.

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father in the heavens.
verse.note: The Greek is plural here and in verse 19, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses constantly. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept here so that the reader hears what a first-century hearer heard.

text.q: And I in turn tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not overpower it.

note.term: you are Peter, and on this rock

verse.note: The Greek plays on the name Peter (Petros) and the word for rock (petra); in Aramaic both would probably be the single word kepha. Whether “this rock” is Peter himself, his confession, or Jesus has been debated since antiquity. Most modern scholars across traditions take it to be Peter in his role as the one who confesses, but the question is not settled.

The nearly universal rendering is “church,” and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer, however, knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so “assembly” is used throughout this translation.

Hades is the realm of the dead, not the place of final punishment. “The gates of Hades” is an Old Testament expression for death (compare Isaiah 38:10). The most common reading is that death will not overcome the community Jesus builds, though some take the gates as an image of hostile powers.

text.q: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of the heavens, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in the heavens, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in the heavens.”

note.term: will be bound in the heavens

verse.note: The Greek construction can also be rendered “will have been bound,” which would mean that Peter’s decisions follow what heaven has already determined, not that heaven ratifies them. Grammarians are divided on whether the form carries that force here. “Bind” and “loose” were used in Jewish teaching for forbidding and permitting, and perhaps also for excluding from and readmitting to the community.

verse.text: Then he gave the disciples strict orders to tell no one that he was the Messiah.
From then on Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.
Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “God forbid, Lord! This will never happen to you.”

note.traditional: Be it far from thee, Lord

verse.note: The Greek is literally “merciful to you,” a compressed idiom from the Greek Old Testament. It is usually understood as “May God be merciful to you,” that is, “God forbid.” Some take it more mildly as “Mercy on you, Lord.” Either way it is a strong exclamation rejecting what has just been said.

verse.text: But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, because your mind is not on the things of God but on the things of people.”
Then Jesus said to his disciples, “If anyone wants to come after me, let them deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow me.

text.q: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake will find it.
For what will it profit a person if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life? Or what will a person give in exchange for their life?

verse.note: Many translations switch from “life” in verse 25 to “soul” here, but the Greek word is the same in both verses, and the argument depends on it. In first-century usage the word most often means a person’s life or living self, not an immaterial part of them. Some translations, such as the NRSV, also keep “life” throughout.

text.q: For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to what they have done.
Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”

verse.note: What event this saying points to is disputed. Proposals include the transfiguration that follows immediately, the resurrection and the spread of the gospel, the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, and the final return of the Son of Man. The translation leaves the wording as open as the Greek.

verse.text: Six days later Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves.
And he was transformed before them: his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as the light.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for a change of form or appearance, and it is the same verb rendered “transformed” in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18. “Transfigured” comes from the Latin translation and survives in English almost only as a name for this event. Nearly all English versions keep “transfigured” here; the plain word is used so that the reader hears what a Greek reader heard and can see the link with Paul’s usage.

verse.text: Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him.
Then Peter spoke up and said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here—one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the everyday one for a tent or hut. The Greek Old Testament uses it both for Israel’s wilderness sanctuary and for the huts of the Feast of Booths, and either association may lie behind Peter’s offer. Older versions have “tabernacles”; modern versions divide between “tents”, “shelters” and “dwellings”.

verse.text: While he was still speaking, suddenly a bright cloud overshadowed them, and there came a voice from the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, the beloved, with whom I am well pleased. Listen to him!”
When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were greatly afraid.
But Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and do not be afraid.”
And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus himself, alone.
As they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Tell no one about the vision until the Son of Man has been raised from the dead.”
And the disciples asked him, “Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?”
He answered, “Elijah is indeed coming, and he will restore all things.
verse.note: The expectation comes from Malachi 4:5–6, where God promises to send Elijah before the day of the Lord to turn the hearts of fathers and children back to one another. The Greek Old Testament uses this same verb, “restore”, in that passage. Jesus affirms the expectation and then, in the next verse, says it has already been fulfilled in John the Baptist.

text.q: But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him but did to him whatever they wanted. In the same way the Son of Man also is about to suffer at their hands.”

verse.text: Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist.
When they came to the crowd, a man approached him, knelt before him,
and said, “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and suffers terribly; he often falls into the fire and often into the water.

note.traditional: is a lunatic; is an epileptic

verse.note: The Greek verb literally means to be affected by the moon, reflecting the ancient belief that the moon’s phases brought on such attacks. The symptoms described, sudden falls into fire and water, are those of a seizure disorder, and many modern versions say “epileptic”. “Has seizures” describes the condition without importing either the ancient theory or a modern diagnosis; verse 18 attributes the boy’s affliction to a demon.

text.q: I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.”

verse.text: Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long will I be with you? How long will I put up with you? Bring him here to me.”
verse.note: The wording echoes the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32:5 and 32:20, where Israel in the wilderness is called a crooked and twisted generation in whom there is no faithfulness. It is not clear whether Jesus is addressing the disciples, the crowd, or his contemporaries as a whole. The Greek word rendered “faithless” is the negative of the word for faith that appears in verse 20.

verse.text: Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed from that hour.
verse.note: The Greek says only “rebuked him” or “rebuked it”, and then “the demon came out of him”. The pronoun could refer to the boy or to the demon, since the form is the same for both. Most translators and commentators take it as the demon, as here, in line with the parallel accounts in Mark and Luke.

verse.text: Then the disciples came to Jesus by themselves and said, “Why could we not cast it out?”

He said to them, “Because of your little faith. For truly I tell you, if you have faith like a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.”

note.term: nothing will be impossible for you

verse.note: Many later manuscripts continue with a verse 21: “But this kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting.” It is absent from important early manuscripts and is widely judged to have been added from the parallel in Mark 9:29, so the Greek text followed here omits it and the numbering passes from 20 to 22. In the same verse, many manuscripts read “unbelief” where the text followed here has “little faith”.

verse.text: As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands,
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s custody or power. The Gospels use it for what Judas, the chief priests and Pilate each do to Jesus in turn, and one English rendering lets that chain be seen. Most versions have “delivered” or “betrayed” here; the lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense, and many scholars regard “betray” as an inference from context, though others defend it where Judas is the subject.

The Greek plays on one word: the “Son of Man” is to be handed over into the hands of “men”, meaning human beings generally. “Human hands” keeps the generic sense while leaving an echo of the wordplay.

verse.text: and they will kill him, and on the third day he will be raised.” And they were greatly distressed.
When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax approached Peter and said, “Does your teacher not pay the two-drachma tax?”
verse.note: The Greek simply says “the two-drachma pieces”. This was the yearly contribution of half a shekel that adult Jewish men paid for the upkeep of the Jerusalem temple, based on Exodus 30:13. Two drachmas was roughly two days’ wages for a laborer. It was a religious levy, not a Roman tax.

verse.text: He said, “Yes.” And when Peter came into the house, Jesus spoke first and said to him, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth collect tolls or poll tax—from their sons or from others?”
verse.note: “Sons” may mean the kings’ own children and household, who are exempt from what the kings levy, or more broadly their own people as opposed to subject foreigners. The first is the more common reading and gives the sharper point: since the tax is for God’s house, God’s children are free of it. On either reading Jesus claims exemption and pays anyway.

verse.text: When he said, “From others,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are free.

text.q: But so that we do not give them offense, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up. When you open its mouth you will find a four-drachma coin. Take that and give it to them for me and for you.”

note.traditional: a piece of money; a shekel

verse.note: The Greek names the coin, a stater, which was worth four drachmas. That is exactly the two-drachma tax for two people, which is why Jesus says it will cover “me and you”.

verse.text: At that time the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Who, then, is greatest in the kingdom of the heavens?”
verse.note: Matthew's Greek has the plural, “the heavens,” which reflects Hebrew and Aramaic idiom and would have sounded Semitic to a Greek ear. Most English translations flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept here wherever the Greek has it; the singular in verse 18 is likewise the Greek's own.

verse.text: He called a child over, set the child in their midst,
and said, “Truly I tell you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of the heavens.

text.q: So whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of the heavens.
And whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.
But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble—it would be better for him to have a donkey millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea.

note.term: causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble

verse.note: The verb means to trip someone up so that they fall in their loyalty to God, whether into sin or out of faith. The older “offend” now suggests hurt feelings, and “cause to sin,” used by some modern versions, is narrower than the Greek. The related noun in verse 7 is rendered “stumbling block.”

Households ground grain with small hand mills; the “donkey millstone” was the large upper stone of a mill turned by an animal. Most translations say “a great millstone” or “a heavy millstone,” which gives the point but not the picture.

text.q: Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks! For stumbling blocks must come, but woe to the person through whom the stumbling block comes!

If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed or lame than to have two hands or two feet and be thrown into the eternal fire.
And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into the Gehenna of fire.

note.traditional: hell fire; the hell of fire

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which in Jewish usage had become the name for the place of final judgment. Many translations render it “hell,” which merges it with Hades and with later imagery. The name is kept here, as in several modern versions.

text.q: See that you do not look down on one of these little ones, for I tell you that their angels in the heavens always see the face of my Father in the heavens.

note.term: the face of my Father in the heavens

verse.note: Verse 11 (“For the Son of Man came to save what was lost”) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not in the Greek text translated here. It was most likely added by copyists from Luke 19:10, and most modern translations omit it or place it in a footnote.

text.q: What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray, will he not leave the ninety-nine on the hills and go and search for the one that is straying?
And if he manages to find it, truly I tell you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine that never went astray.
In the same way, it is not the will of your Father in the heavens that one of these little ones should be lost.
If your brother sins against you, go and point out his fault, between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have won your brother.

verse.note: Some of the earliest manuscripts lack “against you,” so that the saying concerns any sin by a fellow believer and not only a personal wrong. The words may have been added under the influence of verse 21, or dropped by accident. Editors are divided, and the Greek text followed here includes them.

“Brother” here is not a sibling but a fellow member of the community of disciples, as the appeal to “the assembly” in verse 17 shows. The term covered women as well as men, and some translations render it “brother or sister” or “member of the church.”

text.q: But if he does not listen, take one or two others along with you, so that ‘every matter may be established on the testimony of two or three witnesses.’
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly; and if he refuses to listen even to the assembly, let him be to you like a Gentile and a tax collector.

verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is recognizable everywhere.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.

verse.note: The Greek construction can also be read “will have been bound in heaven,” so that the community's decision follows heaven's rather than the reverse; scholars disagree on how much weight the tense will bear. “Binding” and “loosing” are widely understood from Jewish usage as forbidding and permitting, and here, in a context of discipline, perhaps also as excluding and readmitting. The “you” is plural, where the same words in 16:19 are addressed to Peter alone.

text.q: Again, truly I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about any matter they ask for, it will be done for them by my Father in the heavens.
For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst.”

verse.text: Then Peter came up and said to him, “Lord, how many times shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times.
verse.note: The Greek can mean either “seventy-seven times” or “seventy times seven,” and translations are divided. The identical phrase appears in the Greek version of Genesis 4:24, where it stands for the Hebrew “seventy-sevenfold” of Lamech's boast of vengeance, and Jesus is probably echoing and reversing that boast. On either reading the point is forgiveness that does not keep count.

text.q: For this reason the kingdom of the heavens may be compared to a king who wanted to settle accounts with his slaves.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. The story depends on this: the master can order the man and his family sold. A king's slaves could hold high office and handle great sums, which explains the size of the debt. Most older translations, and several modern ones, have “servants.”

text.q: When he began the settling, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents.

verse.note: A talent was the largest unit of money, worth roughly six thousand denarii, and a denarius was about a day's wage for a laborer. Ten thousand was the highest number for which Greek had a single word, so the sum is deliberately beyond any possibility of repayment. The hundred denarii of verse 28 is a real but ordinary debt, about one six-hundred-thousandth of the first.

text.q: Since he had no means to repay, the master ordered him to be sold, along with his wife and children and everything he had, and the debt to be repaid.
So the slave fell to the ground and bowed down before him, saying, ‘Be patient with me, and I will repay you everything.’

verse.note: The Greek verb names prostration in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it. Here a slave prostrates himself before his master to plead for time, so the physical gesture is rendered and not “worship,” as in the King James Version. Most modern translations do the same in this verse.

text.q: Moved with compassion, the master of that slave released him and forgave him the loan.
But that slave went out and found one of his fellow slaves who owed him a hundred denarii, and he seized him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Pay back what you owe.’
So his fellow slave fell down and begged him, saying, ‘Be patient with me, and I will repay you.’
But he refused. Instead he went and threw him into prison until he should repay what was owed.
When his fellow slaves saw what had happened, they were deeply distressed, and they went and reported to their master everything that had happened.
Then his master summoned him and said to him, ‘You wicked slave! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow slave, as I had mercy on you?’
And in his anger his master handed him over to the torturers until he should repay all that was owed.
So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts.”

verse.text: When Jesus had finished saying these things, he left Galilee and went into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan.
Large crowds followed him, and he healed them there.
Some Pharisees came to him to test him, asking, “Is it permitted for a man to divorce his wife for any reason at all?”
verse.note: Older versions have “tempting him.” The Greek verb means to put someone to the test, here by a question meant to trap, and modern English “tempt” has narrowed to enticing someone to sin. Most recent translations also use “test” in this verse.

The question reflects a live dispute over Deuteronomy 24:1, which allows a man to divorce his wife if he finds “something indecent” in her. According to later rabbinic tradition, the school of Shammai limited this to sexual misconduct, while the school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost any fault. The Pharisees are pressing Jesus to take a side.

verse.text: He answered, “Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’

text.q: and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’?
So they are no longer two but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

verse.text: They said to him, “Why then did Moses command us to give a certificate of dismissal and divorce her?”
He said to them, “It was because of your hardness of heart that Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it has not been this way.

text.q: And I tell you, whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.”

verse.note: The Greek word is a broad term for unlawful sexual activity. Most interpreters take it here to mean a wife’s sexual unfaithfulness; others limit it to unchastity before marriage, or to marriages within the forbidden degrees of kinship in Leviticus 18. The exception appears only in Matthew (here and 5:32), and its scope is disputed.

note.term: and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery

verse.note: Many early manuscripts lack this final clause, and several critical editions and modern translations omit it as a possible carry-over from 5:32. The SBLGNT text translated here includes it.

verse.text: The disciples said to him, “If that is how it is for a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.”
But he said to them, “Not everyone can accept this saying, but only those to whom it has been given.
verse.note: “This saying” may point back to Jesus’ teaching on marriage and divorce (verses 4–9) or to the disciples’ remark that it is better not to marry. The second fits the words about eunuchs that follow and is the more common view, but both are defended.

text.q: For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by people, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of the heavens. Let the one who is able to accept this accept it.”

verse.note: Matthew’s Greek has the plural, “the heavens,” a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “the kingdom of heaven.” The phrase means the same as “the kingdom of God,” which Matthew uses in verse 24.

Eunuchs—castrated men, often court officials—were a familiar figure in the ancient world, and the Law of Moses excluded them from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1). The third group is almost universally understood as a figure of speech for those who give up marriage for the sake of the kingdom, not as literal self-mutilation.

verse.text: Then children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them and pray, but the disciples rebuked them.
But Jesus said, “Leave the children alone, and do not stop them from coming to me, for the kingdom of the heavens belongs to such as these.”
And after laying his hands on them, he went on from there.
Just then someone came up to him and said, “Teacher, what good thing must I do to have eternal life?”
He said to him, “Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”

note.term: Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good.
note.traditional: Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one, that is, God,” matching Mark 10:18 and Luke 18:19. The earlier manuscripts have the wording translated here, and the other reading is generally regarded as a harmonization to the parallel accounts.

verse.text: He asked him, “Which ones?” Jesus said, “‘You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not give false testimony.

text.q: Honor your father and mother,’ and ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’”

verse.text: The young man said to him, “I have observed all these. What do I still lack?”
Jesus said to him, “If you want to be complete, go, sell your possessions and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in the heavens. Then come, follow me.”
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “perfect.” The Greek word describes what has reached its goal or lacks nothing—whole, complete, mature—and in the Greek Old Testament it is used of people wholly devoted to God. “Complete” also answers the young man’s question, “What do I still lack?” “Perfect” remains the standard rendering and is defensible, but in modern English it suggests flawlessness.

verse.text: But when the young man heard this, he went away grieving, for he had much property.
Then Jesus said to his disciples, “Truly I tell you, it will be hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom of the heavens.

text.q: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

verse.note: The image is a deliberate exaggeration: the largest animal of the region and the smallest familiar opening. The popular explanation that “the Needle’s Eye” was a small gate in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence behind it. The disciples’ reaction in verse 25 shows they understood the saying to mean “impossible.”

verse.text: When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished and said, “Who then can be saved?”
Jesus looked straight at them and said, “For human beings this is impossible, but for God all things are possible.”
Then Peter responded, “Look, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?”

Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, at the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

note.term: at the renewal of all things

verse.note: The Greek is a single word meaning “rebirth” or “renewal,” used in the period for the restoration of the world or of a nation after catastrophe. Here it refers to the renewed world of the age to come. Older versions have “in the regeneration”; many modern versions have “the renewal of all things” or “the new world.”

text.q: And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or wife or children or fields for the sake of my name will receive a hundred times as much and will inherit eternal life.

verse.note: Some important early manuscripts lack “or wife,” and a few read “many times as much” instead of “a hundred times as much.” Critical editions differ on both points; the SBLGNT text is translated here.

text.q: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.”
“For the kingdom of the heavens is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.

verse.note: Matthew’s Greek has the plural, “the heavens,” reflecting the Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking, in which the word for heaven is plural in form. Most English translations flatten it to “the kingdom of heaven.” The plural is kept here because a first-century hearer would have noticed the Semitic turn of phrase.

text.q: After agreeing with the workers on a denarius for the day, he sent them into his vineyard.

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin and, as the parable itself assumes, an ordinary day’s pay for a laborer. The agreed rate is therefore fair, neither stingy nor generous.

text.q: And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace,

verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the third hour is mid-morning (about nine o’clock), the sixth is noon, the ninth is mid-afternoon, and the eleventh is roughly an hour before the working day ends at sunset. The ancient hour-counts are kept because the story turns on them.

text.q: and to them he said, ‘You go into the vineyard too, and I will give you whatever is just.’

verse.note: The Greek adjective belongs to a single word-family that English splits in two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. “Just” is used here so that the reader hears the link with verse 13, where the landowner uses the matching verb to say he is doing no injustice. Most translations have “whatever is right” here and “I am not wronging you” there.

text.q: So they went. Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same.
And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing there, and he said to them, ‘Why have you been standing here idle all day?’
They said to him, ‘Because no one hired us.’ He said to them, ‘You go into the vineyard too.’
When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his manager, ‘Call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and going on to the first.’
And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, they each received a denarius.
So when the first came, they thought they would receive more; but they too each received a denarius.
When they received it, they began grumbling against the landowner,
saying, ‘These last ones worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’
But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no injustice. Did you not agree with me on a denarius?
Take what is yours and go. I want to give this last one the same as I gave you.
Am I not allowed to do what I want with what is mine? Or is your eye evil because I am good?’

note.term: is your eye evil because I am good
note.traditional: Is thine eye evil, because I am good? (KJV); are you envious because I am generous? (most modern versions)

verse.note: An “evil eye” was a common Jewish idiom for a grudging, envious or stingy attitude toward others, the opposite of generosity (compare Matthew 6:23). Most modern translations paraphrase: “Are you envious because I am generous?” The literal wording is kept so that the idiom and the contrast of “evil” with “good” stay visible; “good” here has the sense of kind or generous.

text.q: So the last will be first, and the first last.”

note.traditional: the first last: for many be called, but few chosen (KJV)

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add “for many are called, but few are chosen,” and the King James Version includes it. The earliest manuscripts lack the words, which were probably brought in from Matthew 22:14. They are not in the Greek text translated here.

verse.text: As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside by themselves, and on the way he said to them,

text.q: “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death,

verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring a person into someone else’s custody or power, and it is used both here and in verse 19. Translations often have “betrayed” where Judas’s act is in view and “delivered” elsewhere, though the lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense.
