One rendering is used throughout so the reader can see the chain of handings-over—to the priests, then to the Gentiles—as a Greek reader did.

text.q: and they will hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and on the third day he will be raised.”

verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural it regularly refers to the non-Jewish peoples, here in practice the Roman authorities. The same word recurs in verse 25. English uses “Gentiles” or “nations” according to context, but in Greek it is one word.

verse.text: Then the mother of Zebedee’s sons came to him with her sons, bowing down before him and asking something of him.
verse.note: The verb names the act of prostrating oneself in reverence, and what it signifies depends on who receives it: it is used of worship offered to God and also of bowing before a king or superior. Here a petitioner approaches with a request and the scene contains no confession of divine status, so the gesture itself is translated, as most modern versions also do. Scholars differ on how much recognition of Jesus’s status Matthew intends in such scenes.

verse.text: He said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right and one at your left, in your kingdom.”
But Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” They said to him, “We can.”
verse.note: In Israel’s Scriptures a cup is a common image for the lot God gives a person to drink, very often suffering or judgment. Jesus uses it here of his coming death (compare Matthew 26:39). The “you” in his reply is plural: he is answering the two sons, not only their mother.

note.term: Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?
note.traditional: …and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with? (KJV)

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add here, and again in verse 23, a clause about being baptized with the baptism Jesus is baptized with, as in the King James Version. The words are absent from the earliest manuscripts and were probably added from the parallel in Mark 10:38–39.

verse.text: He said to them, “My cup you will drink, but to sit at my right and at my left is not mine to give; it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”
When the ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers.
But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones wield authority over them.

text.q: It is not to be so among you. Rather, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant,
and whoever wants to be first among you must be your slave—
just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

verse.note: The Greek noun was the ordinary term for the price paid to free a slave, a captive or something held in pledge. The preposition translated “for” commonly means “in place of” or “in exchange for.” “Many” is a Semitic way of setting the one over against the large number who benefit and need not mean “not all”; many scholars hear an echo of Isaiah 53:11–12.

verse.text: As they were leaving Jericho, a large crowd followed him.
And look, two blind men were sitting beside the road; when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!”
The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the louder, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!”
Jesus stopped and called them and said, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said to him, “Lord, let our eyes be opened.”
Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes, and at once they regained their sight and followed him.
When they had come near Jerusalem and reached Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples,
saying to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied up and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me.

text.q: And if anyone says anything to you, you are to say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and he will send them immediately.”

note.traditional: The Lord hath need of them

verse.note: The Greek word can mean “lord”, “master” or “owner”, and the sentence could also be construed as “their owner needs them”. Most translations and commentators take it as Jesus referring to himself as “the Lord”, and that reading is followed here. The closing words, “he will send them immediately”, are taken as Jesus’ assurance about the person addressed, not as part of the message.

verse.text: This took place so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled:

text.q: “Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Look, your king is coming to you, gentle and mounted on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’”

verse.note: The traditional “meek” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone gentle and humble, not self-assertive; here it marks a king who arrives without military display. Most modern translations use “gentle” or “humble”.

note.term: on a donkey, and on a colt

verse.note: The quotation joins an opening line from Isaiah 62:11 to Zechariah 9:9. In Zechariah’s Hebrew poetry the donkey and the colt are parallel descriptions of a single animal; Matthew’s account, unlike the other Gospels, mentions both a donkey and her colt. A king riding a donkey instead of a war horse signaled a peaceful arrival.

verse.text: The disciples went and did just as Jesus had directed them.
They brought the donkey and the colt and laid their cloaks on them, and he sat on them.
verse.note: “Them” may refer to the cloaks or to the two animals; the Greek does not decide. Most interpreters take it to mean that Jesus sat on the cloaks.

verse.text: Most of the crowd spread their own cloaks on the road, while others were cutting branches from the trees and spreading them on the road.
The crowds that went ahead of him and those that followed were shouting, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest heavens!”
verse.note: The Greek transliterates a Hebrew cry meaning “save, please” from Psalm 118:25, the psalm quoted in the next line. By this period it appears to have become a shout of acclamation as much as a plea, which is why it can be addressed “to the Son of David”. “In the highest heavens” is literally “in the highest places”, traditionally “in the highest”.

verse.text: When he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was shaken, asking, “Who is this?”
And the crowds were saying, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth in Galilee.”
Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who were selling and buying in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.
verse.note: Pilgrims needed to exchange their everyday coins for the currency accepted for the temple tax, and to buy animals fit for sacrifice; doves were the offering of the poor. This trade took place in the outer courts of the temple complex, not in the sanctuary building itself.

verse.text: And he said to them, “It is written, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer,’ but you are making it a den of bandits.”

note.traditional: den of thieves / den of robbers

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a violent plunderer such as a brigand or highwayman, not a thief who steals by stealth, and it was also used of insurgents. “Robbers” is the usual modern rendering and is not wrong; “bandit” keeps the note of violence and outlawry. The phrase echoes Jeremiah 7:11, and the first half of the saying quotes Isaiah 56:7.

verse.text: Blind and lame people came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonders he did and the children shouting in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” they were indignant
and said to him, “Do you hear what these children are saying?” Jesus said to them, “Yes. Have you never read, ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise for yourself’?”
Then he left them and went out of the city to Bethany, and he spent the night there.
Early in the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry.
Seeing a lone fig tree by the road, he went up to it and found nothing on it except leaves. He said to it, “May no fruit ever come from you again!” And the fig tree withered at once.
When the disciples saw it, they were amazed and said, “How did the fig tree wither at once?”

Jesus answered them, “Truly I tell you, if you have faith and do not doubt, not only will you do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen.

text.q: And whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

verse.text: When he had come into the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching and said, “By what authority are you doing these things? And who gave you this authority?”
Jesus answered them, “I too will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, I too will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.
The baptism of John—where was it from? From heaven or from people?” They discussed it among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’

text.q: But if we say, ‘From people,’ we are afraid of the crowd, for they all regard John as a prophet.”

verse.text: So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And he in turn said to them, “Neither am I telling you by what authority I am doing these things.”

text.q: “What do you think? A man had two sons. He went to the first and said, ‘Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’
He answered, ‘I will not,’ but later he changed his mind and went.

verse.note: The manuscripts differ over the order of the two sons in verses 29 to 31. Some early witnesses have the first son say yes and not go and the second refuse and then go, with the answer in verse 31 adjusted to match. The order translated here is that of the SBLGNT and of most modern editions; the point of the parable is the same either way.

text.q: Then he went to the second and said the same thing. He answered, ‘I will, sir,’ and he did not go.

verse.text: Which of the two did the father’s will?” They said, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes are going ahead of you into the kingdom of God.

text.q: For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And you, when you saw this, did not even change your minds later and believe him.”
“Listen to another parable. There was a landowner who planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower. Then he leased it to tenants and went abroad.
When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his slaves to the tenants to collect his fruit.

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Many English versions soften it to “servants”; some modern translations use “slaves”, as here.

text.q: But the tenants seized his slaves; one they beat, another they killed, and another they stoned.
Again he sent other slaves, more than the first, and they treated them the same way.
Last of all he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’
But when the tenants saw the son, they said among themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’
And they seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him.
So when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?”

verse.text: They said to him, “He will bring those evil men to an evil end and lease the vineyard to other tenants, who will hand over the fruit to him in its season.”
Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone that the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone; this came from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?
verse.note: The Greek, quoting Psalm 118:22, is literally “head of the corner”. It may mean the foundation stone at the corner of a building or the capstone that completes the top of a wall or arch; scholars are divided. Either way it is the most important stone in the structure.

text.q: For this reason I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation that produces its fruit.

verse.note: This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually rendered “Gentiles”; in the singular it means a people or nation. Who is meant is debated. Many take it as the community of Jesus’ followers, Jewish and Gentile; others see a new leadership replacing the chief priests and Pharisees who are addressed here.

text.q: And the one who falls on this stone will be shattered, and anyone on whom it falls it will crush.”

note.term: And the one who falls on this stone will be shattered

verse.note: This verse is absent from a few early witnesses, including Codex Bezae and part of the Old Latin tradition, and it closely resembles Luke 20:18. Some scholars therefore think it was copied into Matthew from Luke, and some editions bracket it. The SBLGNT prints it as part of the text.

verse.text: When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they realized that he was speaking about them.
And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet.
Jesus responded by speaking to them again in parables. He said,

text.q: “The kingdom of the heavens may be compared to a king who gave a wedding banquet for his son.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses regularly and that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The meaning is not in dispute: it is Matthew’s way of speaking of God’s reign.

text.q: He sent his slaves to call those who had been invited to the wedding banquet, but they would not come.

verse.note: The Greek word names a person owned by a master, not a hired employee; a king’s household was staffed by such people, some of them of considerable standing. Many English versions soften it to “servants,” though several recent ones use “slaves.” The attendants in verse 13 are a different Greek word and are rendered “servants.”

text.q: Again he sent other slaves, saying, ‘Tell those who have been invited: “Look, I have prepared my dinner; my bulls and fattened cattle have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding banquet.”’
But they paid no attention and went away, one to his own field, another to his business.
The rest seized his slaves, abused them, and killed them.
The king was enraged. He sent his troops, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city.
Then he said to his slaves, ‘The wedding banquet is ready, but those who were invited were not worthy.
So go to where the roads lead out, and invite to the wedding banquet as many as you find.’
So those slaves went out into the roads and gathered everyone they found, both bad and good, and the wedding banquet was filled with guests.
But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw a man there who was not wearing a wedding garment,
and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?’ But the man was left speechless.
Then the king said to the servants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and throw him out into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’
For many are invited, but few are chosen.”

note.traditional: called (“many are called, but few are chosen”)

verse.note: The word is from the same root as the verb used throughout the parable for inviting the guests (verses 3, 4, 8 and 9), so “invited” keeps the closing saying tied to the story it sums up. The traditional “called” is equally accurate, and it is the usual rendering of this word in the letters. Some recent versions also have “invited” here.

verse.text: Then the Pharisees went and plotted together how to trap him in what he said.

They sent their disciples to him, together with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth. You defer to no one, for you pay no regard to people’s standing.
verse.note: The Herodians are mentioned only in the Gospels, and their exact identity is uncertain; the name suggests supporters of the Herodian dynasty, whose rule depended on Rome. Their presence alongside the Pharisees’ disciples sharpens the trap: refusing the tax could be reported as sedition, while endorsing it would offend popular feeling.

text.q: So tell us what you think: Is it permitted to pay the tax to Caesar or not?”

verse.note: The Greek borrows the Latin word census and refers to the head tax Rome levied on its provincial subjects. It was widely resented in Judea as a mark of foreign rule. It was paid in Roman coin, and the denarius of the period typically bore the emperor’s portrait and an inscription naming him as son of the deified Augustus, which is the point of Jesus’ question in verse 20.

verse.text: But Jesus, knowing their malice, said, “Why are you testing me, you hypocrites?
verse.note: The verb means to put someone to the test, here with the aim of trapping him. Older versions have “tempt,” which in modern English suggests enticement to sin; most recent translations use “test” in this passage, as here and in verse 35.

verse.text: Show me the coin used for the tax.” And they brought him a denarius.
He said to them, “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?”
They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “So give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”
verse.note: The questioners asked whether it is permitted to “give” the tax; Jesus answers with a stronger verb that commonly means to pay what is owed or return what belongs to someone. “Render” carries this but is now archaic. The implication that the coin already belongs to Caesar, and that something else belongs to God, is generally recognized.

verse.text: When they heard this they were amazed, and they left him and went away.
That same day Sadducees came to him, saying that there is no resurrection, and they put a question to him:

note.term: saying that there is no resurrection
note.traditional: who say there is no resurrection

verse.note: In the Greek text followed here the phrase has no article, so it most naturally means the Sadducees came asserting that there is no resurrection. Many manuscripts add the article, giving “who say there is no resurrection,” a general description of the group like that in Mark and Luke; many translations render it that way. Either way, denial of resurrection was a known Sadducean position.

text.q: “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies without children, his brother shall marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.’

note.term: his brother shall marry his wife

verse.note: The Sadducees paraphrase the law of levirate marriage in Deuteronomy 25:5, with wording that also echoes Genesis 38:8. Under it a dead man’s brother married the widow, and the first son was counted as the dead man’s heir. The Greek verb is a technical one for marrying as a brother-in-law.

text.q: Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and since he had no offspring he left his wife to his brother.
The same happened with the second and the third, and so on through all seven.
Last of all, the woman died.
In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be, of the seven? For they all had her.”

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.

text.q: For in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels of God in heaven.

verse.note: Manuscripts differ here: some read “angels of God,” others simply “angels.” The edition translated here includes “of God”; other critical editions and many modern translations omit it. The sense is unaffected.

text.q: And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God:
‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead but of the living.”

verse.text: When the crowds heard this, they were astounded at his teaching.
When the Pharisees heard that he had left the Sadducees speechless, they gathered together.
And one of them, an expert in the law, put a question to him, testing him:
verse.note: The word names a man learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with those elsewhere called scribes. “Lawyer,” kept by many versions, now suggests an attorney who represents clients in court. Several modern translations use “expert in the law” or something close to it.

text.q: “Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?”

verse.text: He said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’

text.q: This is the great and first commandment.
A second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
On these two commandments the whole Law hangs, and the Prophets.”

verse.text: While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus put a question to them:
“What do you think about the Messiah? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “David’s.”
verse.note: The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one” and is here a title, the expected king of David’s line, not a name for Jesus. “Messiah” lets the modern reader hear a title, as the Pharisees did. Several modern translations make the same choice in passages like this and keep “Christ” where it functions as a name.

verse.text: He said to them, “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying,

text.q: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet”’?

note.term: The Lord said to my Lord

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:1. In Hebrew the first “Lord” is the divine name and the second is a different word for a master or king; the Greek uses the same word for both. Jesus’ argument rests on premises his hearers shared: that David is the speaker and that the one he addresses is the Messiah, so that David calls his own descendant his superior.

text.q: If, then, David calls him Lord, how is he his son?”

verse.text: And no one was able to answer him a word, and from that day on no one dared to put any more questions to him.
Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples,
saying, “The scribes and the Pharisees have taken their seat on the chair of Moses.
verse.note: A first-century hearer would have understood this as a claim to teach with Moses’ authority as interpreters of the Law. Whether an actual seat of honor in the synagogue is meant or the phrase is purely figurative is debated. Stone seats of this kind have been found in some ancient synagogues, though they may be later than Jesus’ time.

text.q: So do and keep whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do, for they say and do not do.
They tie up heavy loads and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them.
Everything they do, they do to be seen by people: they make their phylacteries broad and their tassels long,

verse.note: Phylacteries (Hebrew tefillin) are small leather cases containing passages of Scripture, strapped to the forehead and arm in obedience to Deuteronomy 6:8. The tassels are those the Law commands Israelites to wear on the corners of their garments (Numbers 15:38–39). Both were ordinary marks of piety, and Jesus himself wore tassels (Matthew 9:20, the same Greek word). The criticism is of enlarging them for show.

text.q: and they love the place of honor at banquets and the foremost seats in the synagogues
and the greetings in the marketplaces, and to be called ‘Rabbi’ by people.
But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi,’ for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers.
And do not call anyone on earth your father, for you have one Father, the heavenly one.
Nor are you to be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Messiah.

verse.note: The Greek word occurs only here in the New Testament. In the usage of the period it meant a teacher or private tutor, so “instructor” fits. Older versions have “master,” and some modern ones have “leader” or “guide,” which leans on the word’s derivation more than on its attested use.

The Greek word is the title of the anointed king Israel expected, and here it carries the article and functions as a title, not a name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader, and several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. Elsewhere, where the word works as a name alongside “Jesus,” this translation keeps “Christ.”

text.q: The greatest among you will be your servant.
Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of the heavens in people’s faces. For you yourselves do not enter, and you do not let those who are entering go in.

verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase characteristic of Matthew that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The meaning is the same.

Many later manuscripts add a further woe here, numbered verse 14: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers; therefore you will receive greater condemnation.” It is absent from the earliest witnesses, and its position varies among those that have it. It is generally judged to have been imported from Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47. The SBLGNT omits it, so the numbering passes from 13 to 15.

text.q: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you travel over sea and dry land to make a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves.

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the name for the place of final judgment. Many translations use “hell,” usually with a footnote, but that merges it with Hades and with later imagery. “Son of” is a Semitic idiom for someone who belongs to or is destined for something.

text.q: Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘Whoever swears by the sanctuary, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the sanctuary is bound.’

verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both render “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building proper, where God was understood to dwell (see verse 21). Most versions use “temple” here; some, such as the NRSV, use “sanctuary” in this chapter. The distinction matters in verse 35, where a murder takes place between the sanctuary building and the altar that stood in front of it.

text.q: You blind fools! Which is greater, the gold or the sanctuary that made the gold holy?

verse.note: The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” and “make holy” keeps that link visible. Most traditional versions use “sanctify,” and some modern ones use “make sacred” or “make holy.” The meaning is not in dispute: the gold and the gift belong to God because of the sanctuary and altar they are attached to.

text.q: And, ‘Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is on it is bound.’
How blind you are! Which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift holy?
So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it;
and whoever swears by the sanctuary swears by it and by the one who dwells in it;
and whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by the one who sits on it.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the Law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

verse.note: The Greek word covers both “faith” and “faithfulness.” Set beside justice and mercy as things to be done, it most naturally means loyalty and reliability, echoing prophetic summaries such as Micah 6:8. Older versions have “faith,” and most modern translations have “faithfulness.”

text.q: Blind guides, straining out the gnat but swallowing the camel!
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside they are full of plunder and self-indulgence.
Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the dish, so that the outside of it may become clean as well.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which on the outside look beautiful but inside are full of the bones of the dead and of every kind of uncleanness.

verse.note: Tombs were marked with white lime so that passersby would not touch them by accident and contract ritual impurity from the dead (Numbers 19:16). Later rabbinic sources describe this being done before festivals. The whitewash made a tomb look bright while marking the uncleanness within.

text.q: So you too on the outside appear righteous to people, but inside you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the memorials of the righteous,
and you say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets.’
So you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets.
You, then, fill up the measure of your fathers!
Snakes! Brood of vipers! How can you escape the judgment of Gehenna?
Therefore, look, I am sending you prophets and sages and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will flog in your synagogues and pursue from town to town,

so that all the righteous blood shed on the earth may come upon you, from the blood of Abel the righteous to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

verse.note: Abel is the first person murdered in Scripture (Genesis 4). The Zechariah meant is most often identified with the priest stoned in the temple court in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22, which is the last such murder in the Hebrew Bible if Chronicles is read as its final book. That Zechariah, however, is called son of Jehoiada, while “son of Barachiah” fits the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1). How the two are related here is disputed, and no explanation is certain.

text.q: Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.
Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her—how often I wanted to gather your children the way a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you did not want it!
Look, your house is left to you desolate.
For I tell you, you will not see me from now on until you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

verse.text: Jesus left the temple and was going on his way when his disciples came up to point out to him the buildings of the temple.
But he answered them, “Do you not see all these things? Truly I tell you, not one stone will be left here on another that will not be thrown down.”
As he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to him privately and said, “Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and the end of the age?”
verse.note: The Greek word means both arrival and presence, and in the period it was a regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. A first-century reader would have heard that royal overtone. Matthew is the only Gospel to use the word, and it recurs in verses 27, 37 and 39.

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “See that no one leads you astray.

text.q: For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Messiah,’ and they will lead many astray.

verse.note: The Greek word is a title meaning the anointed king Israel was expecting, and here pretenders claim it as a title. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader, whereas “Christ” is now heard as a name. Several modern translations make the same distinction in the Gospels.

text.q: You are going to hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must happen, but the end is not yet.
For nation will rise up against nation and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places.

verse.note: A single Greek word lies behind both “nations” and “Gentiles” in English Bibles; in the plural it often means the non-Jewish peoples. In verses 9 and 14 “all the nations” could also be heard as “all the Gentiles”. The worldwide scope of the passage favors “nations”, which is the usual rendering here.

text.q: But all these things are the beginning of the birth pains.
Then they will hand you over to affliction and will kill you, and you will be hated by all the nations because of my name.

verse.note: This is the ordinary Greek verb for passing someone into another’s custody, and Matthew uses the same word for what Judas, the chief priests and Pilate do to Jesus. Most versions vary the English, with “deliver up” here and “betray” in verse 10, and “betray” is a fair inference from the context there. One rendering is kept so that the reader can see the repetition the Greek reader saw.

The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression bearing down on people, not a technical term. Many versions keep “tribulation”, especially “great tribulation” in verse 21, but many readers now hear that as the name of a specific end-time period, which is more than the word itself says. The same word is used in verses 21 and 29.

text.q: And then many will fall away, and they will hand one another over and hate one another.
Many false prophets will rise up and lead many astray.
And because lawlessness will multiply, the love of most will grow cold.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
And this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed in the whole inhabited world as a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come.

verse.note: The Greek was an everyday word for a public announcement of good news, used also of royal and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has become a religious term and the name of a kind of book, so “good news” is closer to what the first readers heard. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

text.q: So when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of through the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—

verse.note: The phrase comes from the book of Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), where it describes a detestable thing set up in the temple that leaves it desecrated and deserted. Jewish readers associated it with the profanation of the temple under Antiochus IV in 167 BC; 1 Maccabees 1:54 uses the same phrase. What event Jesus points to is disputed: many connect it with the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, others with a still future event, others with both.

This may be Jesus’s own words, directing the reader of Daniel to grasp the prophecy, or an aside by the evangelist to the person reading the Gospel (often aloud to a congregation). Many translations mark it as an aside with parentheses. Because Matthew has just named Daniel, it is left here within Jesus’s speech, but the other reading is equally possible.

text.q: then those in Judea must flee to the mountains.
The one on the housetop must not go down to take what is in his house,
and the one in the field must not turn back to take his cloak.
Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days!
Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath.
For then there will be great affliction, such as has not happened from the beginning of the world until now, and never will happen again.
And if those days had not been cut short, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the chosen those days will be cut short.

verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary adjective for someone or something picked out, used in the Septuagint of Israel as the people God chose. “The elect” is the usual English rendering, but it has become a specialized theological term, whereas the first readers heard a plain word. The meaning is not in dispute.

text.q: Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Messiah!’ or ‘Here!’ do not believe it.
For false messiahs and false prophets will rise up and give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the chosen.
See, I have told you beforehand.
So if they say to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness,’ do not go out; or ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe it.
For just as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.
Wherever the carcass is, there the vultures will gather.

verse.note: The Greek word usually means eagle but was also applied to vultures, and birds gathering at a carcass suggests carrion-eaters. Older versions have “eagles”; most modern ones have “vultures”. The saying appears to be a proverb, and its point here is debated; some see an allusion to the eagle standards of the Roman legions, but that is uncertain.

text.q: Immediately after the affliction of those days, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from the sky, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.
And he will send out his angels with a great trumpet, and they will gather his chosen from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other.
Learn the parable from the fig tree: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, you know that summer is near.
So you also, when you see all these things, know that he is near, at the very doors.

verse.note: The Greek has no expressed subject and can equally mean “it is near”, that is, the end or the coming just described. “At the doors” suggests a person arriving, and most translations choose “he”, but several give “it”.

text.q: Truly I tell you, this generation will certainly not pass away until all these things take place.

verse.note: The word normally means the people alive at one time, and that is how Matthew uses it elsewhere. Because this seems to place “all these things” within the lifetime of Jesus’s hearers, some have proposed “this race” or “this kind of people”, while others limit “all these things” to the events leading up to the fall of Jerusalem. The usage of the period supports the plain sense; the difficulty is one of interpretation, not of translation.

text.q: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will certainly not pass away.
But about that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of the heavens, nor the Son, but only the Father.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts lack these words, and some older English versions accordingly omit them. The earliest and most important witnesses include them, and they are probably original; scribes are more likely to have removed a statement that the Son does not know than to have added it. The parallel in Mark 13:32 has the words without significant variation.

text.q: For just as the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.
For as in those days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark,
and they knew nothing until the flood came and swept them all away, so too will be the coming of the Son of Man.
Then two men will be in the field: one will be taken and one left.
Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken and one left.
So keep watch, because you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.
But know this: if the owner of the house had known in what watch of the night the thief was coming, he would have kept watch and would not have let his house be broken into.
For this reason you also must be ready, because the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.
Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household to give them their food at the proper time?

verse.note: The Greek word means a slave, someone owned by a master, not a hired employee, and the first readers would have pictured a slave manager set over the other household slaves. Most English versions soften it to “servant”, though some use “slave”. The word for “master” throughout the parable is the same Greek word translated “Lord” in verse 42.

text.q: Blessed is that slave whom his master finds doing so when he comes.
Truly I tell you, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.
But if that wicked slave says in his heart, ‘My master is taking a long time,’
and begins to beat his fellow slaves, and eats and drinks with the drunkards,
the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know,
and will cut him in two and assign him his place with the hypocrites. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

note.traditional: cut him in pieces; cut him asunder

verse.note: The verb literally means to cut in two, a savage punishment known in the ancient world. Because the slave is afterward assigned a place with the hypocrites, some take it figuratively as “punish severely” or “cut him off”, but a figurative use is not clearly attested elsewhere. The literal rendering is kept; the parable shifts at this point from the story to the judgment it portrays.

text.q: “Then the kingdom of the heavens will be like ten young women who took their torches and went out to meet the bridegroom.

verse.note: Matthew's Greek has the plural, “heavens,” a Semitic turn of phrase that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most English translations flatten it to “heaven”; the plural is kept here wherever the Greek has it.

The Greek word denotes an unmarried girl of marriageable age, who was assumed to be a virgin. Most versions have “virgins” and some “bridesmaids.” In this story the point is the girls' role as young unmarried attendants at the wedding, and “virgins” puts the emphasis in the wrong place for a modern reader. “Bridesmaids” was not chosen because it suggests a modern wedding custom.

The usual meaning of this word is “torch” (as in John 18:3); the ordinary word for a household oil lamp is a different one. Many commentators picture sticks wrapped in oil-soaked rags, carried in a night-time wedding procession, which burn briefly and must be re-soaked from a flask. The word can also mean “lamp,” and most translations and some lexicons take it that way here, so the traditional rendering remains possible.

text.q: Five of them were foolish and five were sensible.

verse.note: The Greek word describes practical good sense and foresight, and is different from the usual word for “wise.” Most translations have “wise” here; “prudent” would also be accurate.

text.q: For when the foolish ones took their torches, they took no oil with them,
but the sensible ones took oil in flasks along with their torches.
When the bridegroom was delayed, they all grew drowsy and fell asleep.
But in the middle of the night there was a shout: ‘Look, the bridegroom! Come out to meet him!’
Then all those young women got up and got their torches ready.
The foolish ones said to the sensible, ‘Give us some of your oil, because our torches are going out.’
But the sensible ones answered, ‘No, there would never be enough for us and for you. Go instead to the dealers and buy some for yourselves.’
But while they were going off to buy it, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.
Later the other young women came too, saying, ‘Lord, lord, open up for us!’
But he answered, ‘Truly I tell you, I do not know you.’
So stay awake, because you do not know the day or the hour.
“For it is like a man about to go abroad, who called his own slaves and handed over his property to them.

verse.note: The Greek word means a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Most English versions soften it to “servants,” though some use “slaves.” Slaves in the ancient world could be given great financial responsibility, as here.

This is the ordinary Greek verb for transferring something into another's control, and it is rendered “hand over” throughout this translation so that the reader can see where the same word recurs. Most versions have “entrusted” or “delivered” here, which is the same sense.

text.q: To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one—to each according to his own ability—and he went abroad. At once

verse.note: A talent was a weight of silver or gold and the largest unit of money in use, worth about six thousand denarii, or roughly twenty years' wages for a day laborer. Even the slave given one talent is handed a very large sum. The English use of “talent” for a natural ability derives from this parable; in the story itself the word means only money.

text.q: the one who had received the five talents went and put them to work and gained five more.
In the same way the one with the two gained two more.
But the one who had received the one went off, dug a hole in the ground, and hid his master’s money.
After a long time the master of those slaves came and settled accounts with them.
The one who had received the five talents came forward and brought five more talents, saying, ‘Master, you handed over five talents to me. See, I have gained five more talents.’
His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful slave! You were faithful over a few things; I will put you in charge of many. Enter into the joy of your master.’
The one with the two talents also came forward and said, ‘Master, you handed over two talents to me. See, I have gained two more talents.’
His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful slave! You were faithful over a few things; I will put you in charge of many. Enter into the joy of your master.’
Then the one who had received the one talent also came forward and said, ‘Master, I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you did not scatter.
So I was afraid, and I went off and hid your talent in the ground. See, you have what is yours.’
But his master answered him, ‘You wicked and lazy slave! You knew, did you, that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter?
Then you ought to have deposited my money with the bankers, and when I came I would have received back what was mine with interest.
So take the talent away from him and give it to the one who has the ten talents.
For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have more than enough; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.
And throw the worthless slave out into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’
“When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne.
All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate people from one another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,

verse.note: One Greek word serves both for “nations” and, in the plural, for “Gentiles,” the non-Jewish peoples. Most interpreters take the phrase here to mean all humanity, as in 24:14 and 28:19, and the translation follows them. Some hold that it means the Gentiles specifically, judged by how they treated Jesus' followers.

text.q: and he will place the sheep on his right and the goats on his left.
Then the king will say to those on his right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me a drink, I was a stranger and you took me in,
naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you looked after me, I was in prison and you came to me.’

verse.note: The verb means going to see someone out of concern for their welfare, and with the sick as object it implies practical care. Most versions keep “visited,” which in modern English suggests no more than a social call. Some versions already have “looked after” or “took care of.”

text.q: Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you a drink?
And when did we see you a stranger and take you in, or naked and clothe you?
And when did we see you sick or in prison and come to you?’
And the king will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, insofar as you did it for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did it for me.’

verse.note: The Greek plural “brothers” regularly includes women. Who is meant is disputed. Elsewhere in Matthew, Jesus' “brothers” are his disciples (12:49–50; 28:10), and many scholars take the phrase here to mean his followers or his messengers. Others take it to mean anyone in need. The Greek does not settle the question.

text.q: Then he will also say to those on his left, ‘Go away from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

verse.note: The same Greek adjective describes the fire here and both the punishment and the life in verse 46. It is related to the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage it often describes what belongs to the age to come, so it is a matter of kind as well as length. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer “of the age to come.”

text.q: For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink,
I was a stranger and you did not take me in, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not look after me.’
Then they too will answer, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not serve you?’
Then he will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, insofar as you did not do it for one of the least of these, you did not do it for me either.’
And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

verse.text: Now when Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples,

text.q: “You know that the Passover comes in two days, and the Son of Man is to be handed over to be crucified.”

verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody. Matthew uses it for what Judas does, what the priests do in taking Jesus to Pilate, and what Pilate does. Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject and “deliver” elsewhere, which hides that one word runs through the whole story. Many scholars regard “betray” as an inference from context and not the word’s meaning, though others defend it for Judas.

verse.text: Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas,
and they plotted together to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him.
But they were saying, “Not during the festival, so that there is no uproar among the people.”
Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper,
verse.note: The familiar byname is kept because it identifies the man; it does not describe his present state. The Greek word covers the range of ritually defiling scaly skin conditions regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which is broader than modern leprosy (Hansen’s disease) and may not include it. Since Simon is hosting a meal, he had presumably recovered and the nickname stayed with him.

verse.text: a woman came up to him with an alabaster jar of very costly perfumed oil, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at the table.
When the disciples saw this, they were indignant and said, “Why this waste?

text.q: This could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor.”

verse.text: Aware of this, Jesus said to them, “Why are you making trouble for the woman? She has done a good deed for me.

text.q: For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.
When she poured this perfumed oil on my body, she did it to prepare me for burial.
Truly I tell you, wherever this good news is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told, in memory of her.”

verse.note: “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, and many modern translations already alternate between the two renderings.

verse.text: Then one of the Twelve, the one called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests
and said, “What are you willing to give me if I hand him over to you?” They weighed out thirty silver coins for him.
verse.note: The verb can mean to place on a scale and so pay out, or to fix or agree on a sum (so the King James, “covenanted with him”). “Weighed out” is chosen because the wording echoes the Greek of Zechariah 11:12, where thirty pieces of silver are weighed out as a shepherd’s wages, a passage Matthew returns to in 27:9–10. Thirty silver shekels is also the compensation set for a gored slave in Exodus 21:32.

verse.text: And from then on he looked for an opportunity to hand him over.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus and said, “Where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?”
He said, “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, ‘The Teacher says, “My time is near. I am keeping the Passover at your house with my disciples.”’”
The disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover.
When evening came, he reclined at the table with the twelve disciples.
And as they were eating, he said, “Truly I tell you, one of you will hand me over.”
Greatly grieved, they began to say to him, one after another, “Surely it is not I, Lord?”
He answered, “The one who has dipped his hand in the bowl with me is the one who will hand me over.

text.q: The Son of Man goes as it is written about him, but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”

verse.text: Judas, the one handing him over, responded, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You have said it.”
verse.note: Literally “You said.” Jesus gives the same reply to the high priest in verse 64. Most scholars take it as an affirmative that leaves responsibility for the words with the questioner; some hear it as more guarded or evasive.

verse.text: While they were eating, Jesus took bread, said the blessing, broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “Take, eat; this is my body.”
Then he took a cup, gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, “Drink from it, all of you,

text.q: for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “of the new covenant,” which is the source of the King James wording. The earliest witnesses lack “new,” which was probably added from Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25. “Blood of the covenant” echoes Exodus 24:8.

text.q: I tell you, from now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.”

verse.text: After singing a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away because of me this night, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’
verse.note: The King James has “be offended,” which now suggests hurt feelings. The verb means to be tripped up so that one’s loyalty fails, and here it refers to the disciples’ desertion later that night; most modern versions likewise have “fall away.” The quotation that follows is from Zechariah 13:7.

text.q: But after I have been raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

verse.text: Peter answered him, “Even if all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.”
Jesus said to him, “Truly I tell you, this very night, before a rooster crows, you will deny me three times.”
Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you.” And all the disciples said the same.
Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to the disciples, “Sit here while I go over there and pray.”
Taking along Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be grieved and distressed.
Then he said to them, “My soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death. Stay here and stay awake with me.”
Going a little farther, he fell on his face and prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will.”
Then he came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “So none of you could stay awake with me for one hour?

text.q: Stay awake and pray, so that you do not enter into testing. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

verse.note: English “temptation” now means enticement to sin, but the Greek word chiefly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will stay faithful—here, the crisis about to break on the disciples. Most versions keep “temptation” in this verse, and a few have “the time of trial.” The lexicons recognize both senses, and the two overlap.

verse.text: Again, a second time, he went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.”
And coming again he found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
So he left them, went away again, and prayed a third time, saying the same words again.
Then he came to the disciples and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Look, the hour has come near, and the Son of Man is being handed over into the hands of sinners.

note.term: Are you still sleeping and resting?
note.traditional: Sleep on now, and take your rest

verse.note: The Greek can be read as a question, as a command (so the King James), or as an exclamation, and a command could be meant ironically. A question is chosen because the next words tell the disciples to get up. The matter remains disputed.

text.q: Get up, let us go. Look, the one handing me over has come near.”

verse.text: While he was still speaking, there came Judas, one of the Twelve, and with him a large crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and elders of the people.
Now the one handing him over had given them a sign, saying, “The one I kiss is the man. Seize him.”
At once he went up to Jesus and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” And he kissed him.
Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you are here for.” Then they came forward, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him.

note.term: do what you are here for

verse.note: The Greek is elliptical, literally “for what you are here.” The King James took it as a question; most recent scholars read it as a clipped command, as here, though “Is this what you have come for?” remains possible. The word rendered “Friend” is a term for an associate that Matthew uses elsewhere in addressing someone who is in the wrong (20:13; 22:12).

verse.text: And suddenly one of those with Jesus stretched out his hand, drew his sword, and struck the slave of the high priest, cutting off his ear.
verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means a slave, a person owned by a master, and that is what a first-century reader would have understood. Many English versions soften it to “servant,” though some, such as the NRSV, have “slave.”

verse.text: Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back in its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword.

text.q: Or do you think that I cannot call on my Father, and he would at once put at my side more than twelve legions of angels?
How then would the Scriptures be fulfilled, which say it must happen this way?”

verse.text: At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest me, as if against a bandit? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me.
verse.note: The Greek word denotes an armed, violent plunderer such as a highwayman, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth; it was also applied to insurgents. Most versions have “robber” (the King James has “thief”), and some render it “rebel” here, which is possible but not certain.

verse.text: But all this has happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets would be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled.
Those who had seized Jesus led him away to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered.
But Peter followed him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the attendants to see how it would end.
Now the chief priests and the whole council were looking for false testimony against Jesus so that they might put him to death,
but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward
and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to tear down the sanctuary of God and to build it in three days.’”
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts (as in verse 55, where Jesus sat teaching) and this one for the building where God was held to dwell. Most English versions do not distinguish them. “Sanctuary” is an accepted rendering that keeps the difference visible, though scholars differ on how strictly the Gospel writers observe it.

verse.text: The high priest stood up and said to him, “Have you no answer? What is it that these men are testifying against you?”
But Jesus stayed silent. And the high priest said to him, “I put you under oath by the living God: tell us if you are the Messiah, the Son of God.”
verse.note: The high priest is asking about a title, the anointed king Israel expected. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “You have said it. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”
verse.note: “The Power” is a reverent Jewish way of referring to God without naming him. The saying combines Psalm 110:1 (seated at God’s right hand) with Daniel 7:13 (one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven), and the high priest hears in it a claim he judges blasphemous.

verse.text: Then the high priest tore his clothes and said, “He has blasphemed! Why do we still need witnesses? Look, now you have heard the blasphemy.
What do you think?” They answered, “He deserves death.”
Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists, and some slapped him,
saying, “Prophesy to us, Messiah! Who is it that hit you?”
Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard, and a slave girl came up to him and said, “You too were with Jesus the Galilean.”
But he denied it in front of them all, saying, “I do not know what you are talking about.”
When he went out to the gateway, another woman saw him and said to those who were there, “This man was with Jesus the Nazarene.”
And again he denied it, with an oath: “I do not know the man.”
After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, “Surely you too are one of them, for your accent gives you away.”
Then he began to call down curses and to swear, “I do not know the man!” And at once a rooster crowed.
verse.note: The verb has no object in the Greek. It is usually understood as Peter calling down curses on himself if he is lying; a minority of scholars suggest that he cursed Jesus. The rendering leaves the object unstated, as the Greek does.

verse.text: And Peter remembered the word Jesus had spoken: “Before a rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” And he went outside and wept bitterly.
When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people conferred together against Jesus, to put him to death.
They bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate the governor.
Then Judas, who had handed him over, saw that Jesus had been condemned. Filled with remorse, he returned the thirty silver coins to the chief priests and elders,
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody, and Matthew uses the same verb for what Judas does, what the priests do to Jesus before Pilate (verse 2), and what Pilate does (verse 26). Most English versions say “betrayed” when Judas is the subject; that names the treachery the context supplies but hides the chain of handings-over. Standard lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense, though some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual meaning.

verse.text: saying, “I have sinned by handing over innocent blood.” But they said, “What is that to us? See to it yourself.”
Throwing the silver coins into the sanctuary, he left; then he went away and hanged himself.
verse.note: Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the sanctuary building itself. It is rendered “sanctuary” here so that the charge in verse 40 and the curtain in verse 51 visibly use the same word. Most versions say “temple”, and this verse is often cited as a looser use of the word, since Judas could not have entered the inner building; he may have thrown the coins toward it or into its precincts.

verse.text: The chief priests took the silver coins and said, “It is not permitted to put these into the temple treasury, since they are the price of blood.”
After conferring together, they used the money to buy the Potter’s Field as a burial place for foreigners.
That is why that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.

Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: “And they took the thirty silver coins, the price of the one on whom a price had been set, on whom some of the sons of Israel had set a price,
verse.note: The wording is closest to Zechariah 11:12–13, where thirty pieces of silver are thrown to the potter in the house of the Lord. Matthew names Jeremiah, most likely because the quotation is blended with themes from that book: the potter, a burial ground linked with innocent blood, and the purchase of a field (Jeremiah 18–19 and 32). The precise explanation is debated.

text.q: and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me.”

verse.text: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned him, saying, “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus said, “You say so.”
verse.note: The Greek is literally “You are saying it.” It can be heard as a plain yes or as a guarded reply (“the words are yours”); it is not a denial. Most interpreters take it as a qualified assent that leaves the meaning of “king” with the questioner.

verse.text: And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.
Then Pilate said to him, “Do you not hear how many things they are testifying against you?”
But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
Now at each festival the governor was in the habit of releasing to the crowd one prisoner, whichever one they wanted.
At that time they were holding a notorious prisoner called Jesus Barabbas.
verse.note: Most manuscripts read simply “Barabbas” here and in verse 17, and most English versions have traditionally followed them. A smaller group of witnesses reads “Jesus Barabbas”, a reading already known to Origen in the third century, and many scholars think the name “Jesus” was original and was dropped by copyists out of reverence. The Greek edition translated here prints the longer reading, which makes Pilate’s question a choice between two men named Jesus.

verse.text: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, “Which one do you want me to release to you: Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Messiah?”
verse.note: The Greek word is a title for the anointed king Israel expected, and Pilate uses it here as a title, not as part of a name. “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” can sound like a surname. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

verse.text: For he knew that it was out of envy that they had handed him over.
While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for today I have suffered a great deal in a dream because of him.”
But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to have Jesus destroyed.
The governor spoke up and said to them, “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” They said, “Barabbas.”
Pilate said to them, “Then what am I to do with Jesus who is called Messiah?” They all said, “Let him be crucified!”
He said, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the louder, “Let him be crucified!”

When Pilate saw that he was getting nowhere, and that a riot was starting instead, he took water and washed his hands in front of the crowd, saying, “I am innocent of this man’s blood. See to it yourselves.”
And all the people answered, “His blood be on us and on our children!”

note.term: His blood be on us and on our children

verse.note: This is a biblical formula for accepting responsibility for a death (compare 2 Samuel 1:16 and Jeremiah 26:15). In the narrative it is spoken by the crowd gathered before Pilate, though Matthew’s word for “the people” is the one he generally uses for Israel as a nation. The verse has a long history of being misused to assign guilt to Jews of every generation, a reading that most interpreters today reject.

verse.text: Then he released Barabbas to them; but Jesus he had flogged, and handed him over to be crucified.
Then the governor’s soldiers took Jesus into the headquarters and gathered the whole cohort around him.
They stripped him and put a scarlet cloak on him,
and they wove a crown out of thorns and put it on his head, and a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, king of the Jews!”
They spat on him, took the reed, and kept striking him on the head.
When they had finished mocking him, they stripped him of the cloak, put his own clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him.
As they were going out, they came upon a man from Cyrene named Simon, and they pressed him into service to carry his cross.
When they came to a place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull,
they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink; but after tasting it, he refused to drink.
When they had crucified him, they divided his clothes among themselves by casting lots,
and sitting down, they kept watch over him there.
Above his head they put the charge against him in writing: “This is Jesus, the king of the Jews.”
Then two bandits were crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left.

note.traditional: robbers (“thieves” in the King James Version)

verse.note: The Greek word denotes someone who robs with violence, such as a brigand or highwayman, and is distinct from the word for a thief who steals by stealth. It was also applied to insurgents, and some translations say “rebels” here; that reading is possible but not certain. Most modern versions use “robbers”.

verse.text: Those passing by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads

note.traditional: reviled (the Greek verb is the source of “blaspheme”)

verse.note: In the period this verb meant abusive speech against anyone, not only against God, whereas modern English “blaspheme” is limited to irreverence toward the divine. Here passers-by jeer at Jesus to his face, so “hurled insults at” gives the sense. English versions vary among “reviled”, “derided” and “hurled insults”.

verse.text: and saying, “You who would destroy the sanctuary and build it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross!”
In the same way the chief priests also, together with the scribes and elders, were mocking him and saying,

text.q: “He saved others; himself he cannot save. He is the king of Israel! Let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him.
He has put his trust in God; let God rescue him now, if he wants him. For he said, ‘I am God’s Son.’”

verse.text: And in the same way the bandits who were crucified with him also taunted him.
From the sixth hour, darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour.
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The word translated “land” can also mean “earth”; whether Matthew means the region or the whole world is not certain.

verse.text: About the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

note.term: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

verse.note: These are the opening words of Psalm 22, which Matthew gives first in a Semitic form (largely Aramaic, with the Hebrew-sounding “Eli”) and then in Greek. The same psalm lies behind the divided clothing, the shaking heads and the taunt in verse 43. “Eli” (“my God”) sounds like a short form of Elijah’s name, which explains the bystanders’ reaction; Elijah was popularly expected to come to the help of the righteous in distress.

verse.text: Some of those standing there heard it and said, “This man is calling Elijah.”
At once one of them ran and got a sponge, filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed, and offered it to him to drink.
But the rest said, “Wait! Let us see whether Elijah comes to save him.”
Then Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit.
And look, the curtain of the sanctuary was split in two from top to bottom. The earth shook, the rocks were split,
the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the holy ones who had fallen asleep were raised;
verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek word means people set apart for God and echoes the Septuagint’s language for Israel; here it refers to the faithful dead. Many translations keep “saints”, and others use “holy people”.

verse.text: and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many.
When the centurion and those with him who were keeping watch over Jesus saw the earthquake and what was taking place, they were terrified and said, “Truly this man was God’s Son!”
verse.note: The Greek has no article and could be read as “a son of a god”, which is how a Roman soldier might naturally have meant it. Matthew’s readers, however, would hear the title used throughout the Gospel and thrown at Jesus in verses 40 and 43, and Greek grammar allows a definite sense without the article. “God’s Son” leaves the phrase about as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: Many women were there, watching from a distance; they had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving him.
Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
When evening came, a rich man from Arimathea arrived, named Joseph, who had himself become a disciple of Jesus.
He went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered it to be given to him.
Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,
and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. Then he rolled a large stone against the entrance of the tomb and went away.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the tomb.
The next day, the one after the Preparation, the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered before Pilate
verse.note: “Preparation” was the usual name for the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday. The day after it is therefore the Sabbath, which Matthew does not name directly as the day the chief priests and Pharisees went to the governor.

verse.text: and said, “Sir, we remember that while he was still alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will be raised.’

text.q: So give orders for the tomb to be secured until the third day; otherwise his disciples may come and steal him and tell the people, ‘He has been raised from the dead,’ and the last deception will be worse than the first.”

verse.text: Pilate said to them, “You have a guard. Go and secure it as best you know how.”
verse.note: The Greek verb can be a statement (“You have a guard”) or a command (“Take a guard”). As a command, Pilate grants them Roman soldiers; as a statement, it may mean the same or may refer them to their own temple police. The word for “guard” is a Latin military term, and in 28:14 the guards are answerable to the governor, which favors Roman soldiers.

verse.text: So they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone and setting the guard.
After the Sabbath, as it was dawning toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to look at the tomb.

note.term: After the Sabbath, as it was dawning toward the first day of the week
note.traditional: In the end of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week

verse.note: The opening word can mean “late on” or “after”, and the verb rendered “dawning” can also be used of a new day “drawing on” at sunset, since the Jewish day began in the evening. A minority therefore place the visit on Saturday evening. Most scholars, comparing the other Gospels, take it as early Sunday morning, as here. “First day of the week” is literally “day one of the Sabbaths”, a Semitic way of counting days from the Sabbath.

verse.text: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, approached, rolled away the stone, and sat on it.
His appearance was like lightning, and his clothing was white as snow.
For fear of him those keeping watch quaked and became like dead men.
But the angel said to the women, “As for you, do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified.

text.q: He is not here, for he has been raised, just as he said. Come, see the place where he was lying.

note.traditional: he is risen / he has risen

verse.note: The Greek verb is passive in form and can mean either “he was raised” (by God) or simply “he rose”. Many translations have “he has risen”. The passive is kept here because the New Testament regularly speaks of God raising Jesus, but both readings are grammatically sound.

text.q: Then go quickly and tell his disciples, ‘He has been raised from the dead, and look, he is going ahead of you to Galilee; there you will see him.’ Look, I have told you.”

verse.text: So they left the tomb quickly, with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples.
And suddenly Jesus met them and said, “Greetings!” They came up to him, took hold of his feet, and worshiped him.
verse.note: The word is the ordinary Greek greeting of the day, as common as “hello”. Its literal sense is “rejoice”, which suits the scene, but a first-century hearer would have taken it first as an everyday greeting.

verse.text: Then Jesus said to them, “Do not be afraid. Go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.”
While the women were on their way, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests everything that had happened.
After the chief priests had met with the elders and formed a plan, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money,
telling them, “Say, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him while we were asleep.’

text.q: And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will win him over and see that you have nothing to worry about.”

note.traditional: if this come to the governor’s ears

verse.note: The Greek is literally “if this is heard before the governor”. That may mean simply that the report reaches him, or more specifically that the matter comes up for a formal hearing in his court. A Roman soldier who slept on watch faced severe punishment, which is why the priests promise to “win him over”, a phrase that may hint at a bribe.

verse.text: So they took the money and did as they were taught. And this story has been spread among Jews to this very day.
verse.note: The Greek has no “the”, so the statement is that the story circulated among Jewish people, not that it was the view of the people as a whole. Most translations supply the article. This is the only place where Matthew’s narrator uses the word outside the title “king of the Jews”.

verse.text: The eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had told them to go.
When they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted.
verse.note: The Greek can mean that some of the eleven doubted, or that they (all of them) worshiped and yet doubted. Most translations and scholars choose “some”. The verb means to waver or hesitate, not to disbelieve outright. Matthew uses it elsewhere only of Peter sinking on the water (14:31).

verse.text: Jesus came up and spoke to them, saying, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.

text.q: Go, therefore, and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,

verse.note: The same Greek word is translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in this translation, where it means the non-Jewish peoples. Here, with “all”, the scope is the whole world, and most scholars take it to include Israel. A minority read it as “all the Gentiles”, marking a turn from the mission to Israel alone in 10:5–6.

The Greek preposition is literally “into”. Some scholars think this signals transfer into the ownership or allegiance of the one named, while others note that “into” and “in” were often interchangeable in the Greek of the period. The traditional “in” is kept because the difference cannot be pressed with confidence.

text.q: teaching them to keep everything I have commanded you. And look, I am with you all the days, until the end of the age.”

verse.note: Most translations have “always”. The Greek says “all the days”, a Semitic turn of phrase that suggests presence day by day up to the end, and it is kept here as written.

Older English versions have “the end of the world”. The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, and the phrase reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. Most modern translations also have “age” here.
